name: Anna Mahizhnan
work: President of the Periyar Ambedkar Thoughts Circle of Australia (PATCA), which campaigns for caste discrimination to be recognised in Australian law.
story: Dr Anna Mahizhnan is president of the Periyar Ambedkar Thoughts Circle of Australia (PATCA) [1]. PATCA is a group named after Periyar and Ambedkar that works against caste discrimination in Australia and has made submissions to federal and state governments [2]. It says it sent more than 30 submissions to the Australian Human Rights Commission in 2022 and has asked New South Wales to make caste a protected attribute in law [3]. When the Commission's National Anti-Racism Framework recognised caste discrimination in November 2024, she called it a major win for caste-oppressed communities and said PATCA was ready to help put it into practice [1].

name: Dr. Ambedkar International Mission (AIM) Australia
work: Volunteer community group that teaches Ambedkar's ideas, promotes his Buddhism and campaigns for caste discrimination to be banned in Australian law.
story: AIM Australia is a not-for-profit community group, part of the worldwide Dr. Ambedkar International Mission network, whose work includes teaching Ambedkar's ideas, campaigning for equality and promoting Navayana (Ambedkar's form of Buddhism) [1]. In 2016, Dr Rupali Bhamare of Melbourne spoke for the group about Ambedkar's life when Western Sydney University's law school received a bust of him [2]. In March 2024 it held a free day of talks at Fed Square in Melbourne for Ambedkar's 133rd birth anniversary, with speakers from Australia and India [3]. Together with the Shri Guru Ravidass Sabha, it led the study 'Caste in Australia', funded by the Australian Human Rights Commission, in which 146 people from caste-oppressed communities were interviewed [4]. The group says it is pushing for Australia's Racial Discrimination Act 1975 to name caste discrimination clearly [1].

name: Mitra Pariyar
work: Nepali Dalit anthropologist who studies caste among Nepali migrants abroad and argues in Nepal's press for Ambedkar's ideas.
story: Mitra Pariyar is a Nepali Dalit rights activist and anthropologist who studied at Oxford and has worked at universities in Australia and England (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. He began reading Ambedkar seriously while doing an anthropology degree at Oxford in late 2008 [1]. His research follows Nepali migrants abroad, including Gurkha soldiers' families settling in Britain and Nepali migrants in Australia [2][3]. His 2019 study found that caste had gained new life overseas, helped along by the internet and smartphones [2]. In Nepal's newspapers he argues that Ambedkar's ideas offer Nepali Dalits their best hope for equality [1].

name: Vikrant Kishore
work: Australian filmmaker and academic whose documentary Resisting Casteism in Australia records Dalit experiences of caste in the diaspora.
story: Vikrant Kishore is an Australian filmmaker, journalist and academic who teaches as an associate professor at the University of Nottingham Ningbo China [1][2]. He helped form a group of academics and activists in Australia that asked the Australian Human Rights Commission to include caste discrimination in its National Anti-Racism Framework [1]. His documentary Resisting Casteism in Australia follows him for about 3,500 km through Melbourne, Sydney, Newcastle and Coffs Harbour to hear Dalit voices, and it was set to premiere at the Melbourne Documentary Film Festival in July 2026 [2]. He has spoken publicly about the caste questions he has faced in Australia, including an incident in 2006 while he was teaching there [3][4]. He also offers free advice to Bahujans (people from communities kept low by caste) who plan to study or work in Australia [1].

name: Anne Murphy
work: Canadian scholar who leads the Caste in Canada project, recording the stories of Ambedkarite and anti-caste community members.
story: Anne Murphy is a scholar at the University of British Columbia whose research covers Punjabi language and history in British Columbia, memories of the 1947 Partition and the Komagata Maru ship incident [1]. From 2020 to 2023 she led a project called Caste in Canada, which profiles and interviews community members, followed by a second phase called The Elimination of Caste from 2024 to 2026 [1]. The project features activists such as Jai Birdi and the late writer Mohan Lal Karimpuri, who spread Ambedkar's teachings through poetry and activism after moving to Canada in 2006 [1][2]. It also funds a postdoctoral fellowship in Dalit studies for 2024 to 2026, helping train new researchers (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. Its recorded interviews create a public record of how Ambedkarites have organised in Canada [1][2].

name: Jai Birdi
work: Social services manager who leads the Chetna Association of Canada, winning Ambedkar memorials, lectures and city proclamations in British Columbia.
story: Jai Birdi came to Canada with his family in the mid-1970s, settled on the west coast in the early 1980s and built a career in social services, rising to senior management [1]. He says his interest in caste barriers grew from curiosity rather than from facing caste oppression himself, and he led the volunteer efforts that became the Chetna Association of Canada, where he is executive director [1]. He helped place memorials to Ambedkar, including a bust at Simon Fraser University, started a Dr. Ambedkar memorial lecture series and persuaded local governments to issue proclamations honouring Ambedkar [1]. In May 2024 he helped steer a gathering of more than 200 delegates on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, where MPs made statements about Ambedkar in the House of Commons [2]. He hopes to see caste added as a protected category in Canadian law and to build a centre guided by Ambedkar's philosophy [1].

name: Christophe Jaffrelot
place: Paris, France and London, United Kingdom
work: French political scientist whose book on Ambedkar and untouchability reached readers from India to Hungary.
story: Christophe Jaffrelot is a French political scientist who studies caste and democracy in India and has taught at Sciences Po in Paris and at King's College London's India Institute [3][4]. Hurst published his book Dr Ambedkar and Untouchability in 2005, which looks at Ambedkar as a thinker about society, as a statesman and as a critic of caste who turned to Buddhism [1]. His French book on Ambedkar and India's Dalits inspired the Hungarian sociologist Tibor Derdák, who saw parallels with the Roma and went on to help found Europe's Ambedkar school [2]. In 2022 he co-edited Ambedkar in London with William Gould and Santosh Dass [3]. He continues to speak publicly about Ambedkar's ideas, including at a Sciences Po discussion in 2024 [4].

name: Nicolas Jaoul
work: French anthropologist who studied why Dalit villages in Uttar Pradesh raise statues of Ambedkar and what those statues mean to them.
story: Nicolas Jaoul is a French anthropologist (a scholar who studies how people live) linked to the Centre for Indian and South Asian Studies at the EHESS research school in Paris [1]. He studied why Dalit communities in Uttar Pradesh put up so many statues of Ambedkar, looking at how the statues spread and what they mean to the people who gather around them (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. His 2006 paper on Dalits, Ambedkar statues and the state appeared in the journal Contributions to Indian Sociology [1][2]. Columbia University, where Ambedkar studied, lists the paper in its online exhibition on caste and Ambedkar [2].

name: Maren Bellwinkel-Schempp
work: German anthropologist who spent decades studying Dalit life and Ambedkarite Buddhism in Kanpur and wrote on Ambedkar studies in Germany.
story: Maren Bellwinkel-Schempp was a German social anthropologist trained at Heidelberg University's South Asia Institute, whose research and solidarity work were devoted to India's Dalits (people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. From 1972 she did fieldwork among Dalits in the industrial city of Kanpur [1]. In a 2007 article titled 'From Bhakti to Buddhism: Ravidas and Ambedkar', she traced how Kanpur's Dalits came to honour the saint Ravidas and then, in the 1980s, accepted Buddhism, which took shape there through a temple, a monk, a lay committee and its own rites [2]. In a 2003 report she described Ambedkar studies at Heidelberg and noted that Ambedkar was gaining recognition in German academic and political circles [3]. She died in Stuttgart in July 2011 [1].

name: Martin Fuchs
work: Professor at the University of Erfurt who studies Dalit movements and writes on Ambedkar's social thought and Buddhism.
story: Martin Fuchs has been professor of Indian religious history at the Max Weber Centre of the University of Erfurt since 2009 [1]. His research covers social and religious movements in South Asia, Dalits, city life and human rights [1]. He has written about Ambedkar's ideas, including a 2019 chapter on Ambedkar's view of the Dhamma (the Buddha's teaching) and the common good, and a 2021 essay on Ambedkar's theory of the social [1]. In July 2024 he gave the closing talk, on Ambedkar's analysis of Indian society and his plan for India's ethical rebuilding, at an Erfurt symposium on Buddhism and the 'untouchables' [2].

name: János Orsós
work: Roma activist who found in Ambedkar a model for his people and co-founded the Jai Bhim Network and its Ambedkar school.
story: János Orsós is a Roma activist from Hungary who spent years trying to keep Roma teenagers from dropping out of school (Roma — a minority people who face heavy discrimination in Hungary) [1]. He first came across Ambedkar at about the age of 25 and felt that Ambedkar's fight against caste and exclusion matched Roma lives more closely than Gandhi's ideas did [1]. He visited Dalit Buddhist schools in India in 2005, became a Buddhist with Tibor Derdák in Nagpur in 2006, and together they started the Jai Bhim Network [1][2]. He is the network's president, and alongside the Dr. Ambedkar School it runs social work, a Buddhist scout troop, choirs and a small farm [3]. Before the school opened, only two Roma students from the Sajókaza area had ever finished high school [1].

name: Tibor Derdák
work: Hungarian sociologist who co-founded the Dr. Ambedkar School, using Ambedkar's life to help Roma teenagers finish school.
story: Tibor Derdák is a Hungarian sociologist and former member of parliament who started schools in the 1990s for Roma teenagers, a minority people who face heavy discrimination in Hungary, where only about 5 percent of Roma children finish secondary school compared with about 80 percent of other children [1]. After reading a French book about Ambedkar and India's Dalits (people the caste system treated as 'untouchable'), he saw parallels with the Roma and travelled to Maharashtra with János Orsós in 2005 to learn from Ambedkarite movements [1]. The two became Buddhists at a mass conversion in Nagpur in 2006, founded the Jai Bhim Network and soon opened the Dr. Ambedkar School in the village of Sajókaza [1]. The school later moved to the city of Miskolc, and in 2023 it taught 125 Roma students in grades nine to twelve [1][2]. As its director, Derdák says Ambedkar's story helps students build a positive picture of themselves, and the school follows his motto of educate, agitate, organise [2].

name: Bhadant Arya Nagarjuna Surai Sasai
work: Japanese-born Buddhist monk in Nagpur who carries on Ambedkar's conversion movement and heads the Deekshabhoomi memorial committee.
story: Surai Sasai is a Japanese-born Buddhist monk who has lived in India since 1967 and works from Nagpur [1]. Japanese researchers describe him as the monk who took a leading role in carrying on the Buddhist conversion movement that Ambedkar began, and their four-year study, finished in 2020, archived more than fifty years of his writings [4]. On 25 December 2016 at Deekshabhoomi he gave initiation into Buddhism to thousands of people from across Maharashtra and read out the 22 vows that Babasaheb had taken at the same place about sixty years earlier [1]. In 2002 he led about 200 monks in a protest at the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, asking that its management be handed to Buddhists [2]. He is president of the Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Smarak Samiti, the Deekshabhoomi memorial committee, and sat on the stage when millions gathered there for the 70th anniversary of the conversion in October 2026 [3].

name: Gail Omvedt
work: American-born sociologist who made a Maharashtra village her home and wrote over 25 books on caste, Ambedkar and anti-caste movements.
story: Gail Omvedt was born in the United States and earned a sociology doctorate at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1973 with a thesis on the anti-caste non-Brahman movement in western India [1]. She made the village of Kasegaon in Maharashtra her home from the 1970s and became an Indian citizen in 1983 [1][2]. She wrote more than 25 books, including Dalits and the Democratic Revolution, Understanding Caste and studies of Ambedkar and of the reformer Jotirao Phule [1]. Berkeley remembered her as both a scholar and an activist in the Ambedkarite movement [1]. She died at her home in Kasegaon in August 2021, aged 81 [1][3].

name: Dhammachari Lokamitra
work: London-born Buddhist teacher who built Nagaloka in Nagpur, training young Ambedkarite Buddhists from across India in Buddhism and social action.
story: Born Jeremy Goody in London in 1947, Lokamitra was ordained into a Western Buddhist order in 1974 and moved to India the following year, arriving on the anniversary of Ambedkar's mass conversion to Buddhism [1]. He set up schools in poor neighbourhoods and in 1998 founded the Jambudvipa Trust to help people from disadvantaged communities take charge of their own progress [1]. He has carried forward Nagaloka, a campus in Nagpur whose first building opened in 1997 and which has a monument to Ambedkar [2]. Its one-year live-in course on Buddhism and social action trained 1,303 young people from 25 Indian states between 2002 and 2018 [2]. His work follows Ambedkar's approach of joining material progress with Buddhist practice [1].

name: Om Prakash Gahatraj
work: Nepali Dalit writer and editor who keeps the history of Nepal's Ambedkarite movement and urges Dalits to follow Ambedkar's path.
story: Om Prakash Gahatraj is a Nepali Dalit writer and organiser described as a walking encyclopedia of Nepal's Ambedkarite movement (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. He worked alongside the veteran leader Mohan Lal Kapali, who showed Ambedkar around Kathmandu's Dalit neighbourhoods during his 1956 visit, and he later wrote Kapali's biography [1]. In the 1980s he was chief editor of Pratinidhi, a Dalit literary magazine that came out four times a year, and he has written many newspaper articles [1]. He has also worked in several roles with Nepal's government on Dalit issues [1]. In a 2014 interview he argued that following Ambedkar's philosophy is the only way to end caste discrimination and untouchability in Nepal [1].

name: Pradeep Manikrao Dhawale
work: President of one of the Ambedkar International Mission groups among Indians in Oman.
story: Pradeep Manikrao Dhawale is president of one of two Ambedkar International Mission groups in Oman [1]. In April 2018 he spoke at a celebration of Ambedkar's 127th birth anniversary at the Embassy of India in Muscat [1]. Both missions came with their members, and the other mission's president, Suryakant Kirloskar, also spoke [1]. The event drew Indian community members and school students, some of whom gave talks on Ambedkar's life and work [1].

name: Park Kyoung-joon
work: Korean Buddhist studies professor who has published a study of Ambedkar's view of Buddhism in Korean.
story: Park Kyoung-joon is a professor in the Faculty of Buddhist Studies at Dongguk University in South Korea [1]. In 2017 he published a Korean-language study of Ambedkar's view of Buddhism, based on Ambedkar's last book, The Buddha and His Dhamma [1]. The article explains how Ambedkar reread Buddhist teachings and wanted the Sangha (the community of monks) to work for society, not only for personal freedom [1]. It also looks at criticisms of Ambedkar's reading and argues that his Buddhism should grow beyond a movement for Dalits into a Buddhism for all people [1].

name: Ravi Chand
work: Dubai-based Indian who founded Ambedkar Global, a group that aims to spread Ambedkar's teachings around the world.
story: Ravi Chand is an Indian living in Dubai who formed Ambedkar Global, an international group that aims to spread Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's teachings worldwide [1]. In 2021 the group held an online event to mark Ambedkar's 130th birth anniversary, with guest speakers from India [1]. Chand said Ambedkar Global was working towards a course on Ambedkar and Ambedkar chairs at universities around the world [1]. Among Indians in the UAE he is also known for arranging several repatriation flights to India during the COVID-19 pandemic [1].

name: Arun Kumar
work: Founder member and long-time general secretary of Britain's main Ambedkarite federation and of the Ambedkar Mission Society in Bedford.
story: Arun Kumar moved to Britain in 1977 after working in government service in Chandigarh, and later worked for Royal Mail in Bedford, a town with an early and active Ambedkarite community [1]. He has been part of the Federation of Ambedkarite and Buddhist Organisations UK since its beginnings in the mid-1980s and served as general secretary of the federation and of the Ambedkar Mission Society in Bedford [1][2]. Groups he worked with have given Ambedkar statues and busts to universities, including the London School of Economics, Columbia University in New York and Simon Fraser University in Canada [1][2]. He has also helped record the movement's history, through long interviews and a chapter he co-wrote with Santosh Dass for the book Ambedkar in London [1][3]. FABO describes this work as keeping Babasaheb's legacy alive beyond India's borders [2].

name: Asang Wankhede
work: Legal researcher who led the 'Caste in Australia' study that helped Australia's human rights body recognise caste discrimination.
story: Asang Wankhede is a postdoctoral researcher at the King's India Institute, King's College London, working on constitutional and anti-discrimination law [1]. As a law doctoral student at Oxford, he led 'Caste in Australia: A phenomenology of casteism', a study led by the Shri Guru Ravidass Sabha and the Ambedkar International Mission [2]. The team interviewed 146 people from caste-oppressed communities and found caste discrimination in schools and universities, workplaces and social life in Australia's South Asian community [2]. Oxford reported in 2025 that his report led the Australian Human Rights Commission to include caste-based discrimination in its National Anti-Racism Framework [3]. He has also done unpaid advocacy for Dalit organisations and spoken against caste discrimination at UN human rights meetings [1].

name: Chakravarty Gautam
work: Co-founder of FABO UK and of the Ambedkar Centre in Southall, who also runs a school for tribal children in Gujarat.
story: Born in Gujarat, Chakravarty Gautam moved to Britain in 1969, built a business and became one of the founders of the Federation of Ambedkarite and Buddhist Organisations UK [1]. In 1993 he and his friends set up the Ambedkar Centre and Buddha Vihara (a Buddhist meeting place) in Southall, west London, which many visiting Ambedkarites now treat as a place of pilgrimage [1]. He started a yearly silent walk from Ambedkar's former London home to the London School of Economics, where Ambedkar studied [1]. In India he founded the Dr. Ambedkar Memorial Trust in Valod, in Gujarat's Tapi district, which runs a school for Adivasi (Indigenous tribal) children and other welfare projects [1]. In 1995 he also helped a BBC crew that was filming a documentary on Ambedkar's life [2].

name: Chanan Chahal
work: Early Bedford organiser who challenged caste insults, embraced Buddhism publicly and wrote a rebuttal to claims that caste bias did not exist in Britain.
story: Chanan Chahal was one of the first Ambedkarite organisers in Bedford, England, where he stood in a local election for a British group linked to the Republican Party of India and helped found local community bodies [1]. In the 1970s he led a boycott of a shop after a caste insult, showing that people would not accept being looked down on because of their birth [1]. In the mid-1980s he publicly became a Buddhist, a step that was covered on BBC television [1]. He wrote a Punjabi book explaining why he was not a Hindu, and when the Hindu Council UK argued that caste discrimination did not exist in Britain, he replied with a report called The Evils of Caste while serving as president of FABO UK [1][2]. He died in 2009, and fellow Bedford activist Ram Pal Rahi pledged to carry on his work [3].

name: Kenneth Griffith
work: Welsh actor and filmmaker who made one of the first television documentaries on Ambedkar's life for the BBC.
story: Kenneth Griffith was a Welsh actor and documentary maker who became curious about Ambedkar while filming in India in the late 1980s, after noticing his statues in Dalit neighbourhoods (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. His plan for a film on Ambedkar's life stalled when Indian officials refused him a visa in 1989, and Ambedkarite groups in Britain passed a resolution backing him [1][3]. The BBC finally paid for the film, which was shot partly in 1995 and shown on BBC Two as The Untouchable – The Life of Babasaheb Ambedkar [1]. Griffith also chaired the International Ambedkar Institute in Britain, a group for research and lectures on Ambedkar, and remained its president until his death in 2006 [1][2].

name: Meena Dhanda
work: Philosopher whose interviews and reports on caste among British South Asians fed into the campaign to add caste to equality law.
story: Meena Dhanda came to Britain from Punjab in 1987 as a Commonwealth Scholar at Oxford and became a philosopher at the University of Wolverhampton [1]. Since 2007 she has interviewed young people in Wolverhampton and Punjab about caste, finding that some Dalit students were treated differently by friends once their caste became known (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1][2]. In 2013–14 the Equality and Human Rights Commission asked her to lead a study called Caste in Britain, to inform whether caste should be covered by the Equality Act 2010 [1][2]. Her university reports that she shared her findings with members of the House of Lords during the 2013 debates and that CasteWatch UK praised her commitment to the cause [2]. Her writing builds on Ambedkar's point that marrying only inside one's own group is what keeps caste going, and she compares casteism with racism [1][3].

name: Ram Pal Rahi
work: A factory worker, taxi driver and driving instructor who gave fifty years of spare time to Ambedkarite and Buddhist groups in Britain.
story: Ram Pal Rahi was born in Punjab in 1954 and reached England in 1975, where he worked at a car factory and then as a security guard, taxi driver and driving instructor [1]. From 1976 he gave his free time to Ambedkarite and Buddhist groups in Bedford, and in 1986 he and his family became Buddhists, following the path Ambedkar opened in 1956 [1]. Over the years he led the Federation of Ambedkarite Buddhist Organisations UK, the Ambedkar Mission Society in Bedford and the Punjab Buddhist Society UK [1]. He helped pay for and finish Buddhist centres in Punjab and travelled across Europe, North America, Malaysia and Japan for Ambedkarite events [1]. He died in Bedford in May 2026 [1].

name: Santosh Dass
work: Campaigns to outlaw caste discrimination in Britain and to honour Ambedkar's London years through a museum, a portrait and a book.
story: Santosh Dass came to Britain from Punjab at the age of eight, grew up in a Dalit family (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') and later worked as a senior civil servant [1]. As president of the Federation of Ambedkarite and Buddhist Organisations UK, she proposed that the Maharashtra government pay for 10 King Henry's Road, the house where Ambedkar lived as a student, which later became the Ambedkar Museum [1][2]. She also pushed for a room and a portrait of Ambedkar at Gray's Inn, where he qualified as a barrister (a courtroom lawyer), and the portrait was unveiled in 2021 [2][3]. As chair of the Anti Caste Discrimination Alliance, she argues that caste should be its own protected category in British equality law [4]. In 2022 she co-edited Ambedkar in London, a book about his student years in the city and about the British Ambedkarite movement [5].

name: Eleanor Zelliot
work: American historian whose pioneering research made the Ambedkar movement and Dalit writing known to scholars and students worldwide.
story: Eleanor Zelliot was an American historian, born in 1926, who taught at Carleton College in Minnesota from 1969 to 1997 and helped start its South Asian studies programme [1][3]. Her doctoral thesis from the late 1960s was among the first academic studies of the Dalit movement after Ambedkar's death (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [2]. She wrote more than eighty articles and several books on the Ambedkar movement, the Buddhist movement he inspired and the poet-saints of Maharashtra, including From Untouchable to Dalit [1]. Her book Ambedkar's World, based on that early thesis, was published in India in 2013 [1][2]. She led student programmes in India several times and kept advising students after she retired, until her death in June 2016 [1].

name: Gary Michael Tartakov
work: American art historian who studies the new Buddhist and Ambedkarite images that Dalits created after 1956.
story: Gary Michael Tartakov is an American art historian and emeritus professor at Iowa State University who studies the art of ancient and modern India [3]. In a 1990 journal article he traced the rise of a new Buddhist imagery among Ambedkar's followers [2]. He edited Dalit Art and Visual Imagery, published by Oxford University Press in 2012, which looks at temples, posters, photographs, statues and parade floats made by, for and against Dalits (Dalit — people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') [1]. The book asks how Dalits have used images of the Buddha and Ambedkar to build a new identity since the 1956 conversion and to draw national attention to their struggle for equal rights [1]. He presented this work in a public lecture at Iowa State in 2013 [3].

name: Jon Keune
work: American religion scholar who studies how Ambedkarite Buddhists from India connect with Buddhists in Japan and Taiwan.
story: Jon Keune is an associate professor of religious studies at Michigan State University in the United States [1]. As a visiting scholar at National Taiwan University's Asian research centre, he has studied religion and migration in Taiwan [1]. His research looks at how, over the past thirty years, migration and shared projects have brought Ambedkarite Buddhists from India into closer contact with Buddhists in Japan and Taiwan [1]. He examines how these groups handle their differences while working together toward their own goals, a sign of how Ambedkar's Buddhism now travels across Asia [1].

name: Kevin D. Brown
work: African American law professor who has spent three decades linking the Black freedom struggle with Dalit rights and caste law.
story: Kevin Brown is an African American law professor who taught at Indiana University's law school from 1987 and joined the University of South Carolina in 2022 [1]. He has spent about 30 years working for justice for Dalits, people the caste system treated as 'untouchable', a commitment shaped by a 1996 visit to Delhi [1]. He writes about how American anti-discrimination law could protect Dalits in the United States, and he worked with lawyers involved in a caste discrimination case against the tech company Cisco [1][2]. He has taught law students in Bangalore and notes that Dalit thinkers have long admired the African American struggle for freedom [1][2]. He recommends Ambedkar's Annihilation of Caste as the place to begin understanding anti-caste thought [2].

name: Ram Kumar
work: President of the Ambedkar International Center, which raised the Statue of Equality near Washington, D.C., and backs anti-caste laws.
story: Ram Kumar is president of the Ambedkar International Center, a nonprofit started in 2012 to spread Ambedkar's ideas about social equality in the United States [1]. In October 2023 the center unveiled a 19-foot statue of Ambedkar called the Statue of Equality, made by sculptor Ram Sutar, on its 13-acre site in Accokeek, Maryland, near Washington, D.C [1][2].. More than 500 people attended, and the center plans a library, a convention centre and a Buddha garden on the land [2]. Kumar said the statue's name reflects the fact that inequality exists in many forms everywhere, not only in India [2]. The center also worked with Seattle councilmember Kshama Sawant and other groups on drafting the city's 2023 ban on caste discrimination [3].

name: S. Karthikeyan
work: Software engineer and founding member of the Ambedkar King Study Circle, a volunteer anti-caste group in Silicon Valley.
story: S. Karthikeyan is an IT engineer in California's Silicon Valley who was earlier active in India's free software movement and organised a national seminar on job reservations in private companies [1]. He is a founding member of the Ambedkar King Study Circle, which brings together the ideas of Ambedkar and the American civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., and a 2026 podcast introduced him as its convenor [1][3]. The circle uses the motto Educate, Organize and Agitate and works to end caste discrimination in India, the United States and elsewhere [2]. It runs reading sessions, an anti-caste helpline, comics and toolkits, and yearly conferences, the seventh of which took place in Fremont, California, in 2026 [2]. It is a members' organisation in which volunteers decide its direction [2].

name: Scott R. Stroud
work: American scholar who wrote an intellectual biography tracing how Ambedkar learned from, and moved beyond, his teacher John Dewey.
story: Scott Stroud is an American scholar of communication at the University of Texas at Austin who studies how Ambedkar used words and arguments to reshape society [1]. His 2023 book The Evolution of Pragmatism in India follows Ambedkar from the philosopher John Dewey's classes at Columbia University in 1913–1916 to his retelling of Buddhist history in the 1950s [1]. The book shows both what Ambedkar took from Dewey and where he broke away to build his own answers to India's problems [1]. An Indian edition was published as An Intellectual Biography of B.R. Ambedkar [3]. In 2023 Stroud also reviewed the book Ambedkar in London for the London School of Economics history blog [2].

name: Thenmozhi Soundararajan
work: Dalit American organiser who founded Equality Labs to fight caste discrimination among South Asians in the United States.
story: Thenmozhi Soundararajan grew up in the United States after her parents left Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu because of caste discrimination (caste — an inherited ranking of families by birth) [1]. In 2015 she founded Equality Labs, which works against caste oppression, gender violence and religious intolerance among South Asians, and she says Ambedkar's work inspires her [1][2]. News reports on caste in America often cite Equality Labs research, and she praised California State University's 2022 decision to ban caste discrimination on all its campuses [3]. Equality Labs was also one of the groups that helped draft Seattle's 2023 proposal to ban caste discrimination [4]. In 2025 the Tamil Nadu government gave her its Vaikom Award for social justice [1].

name: Yashica Dutt
work: Journalist and author of the memoir Coming Out as Dalit, who writes and speaks about caste in India and in the United States.
story: Yashica Dutt was born into a Dalit family (Dalits are people the caste system treated as 'untouchable') in Ajmer, Rajasthan, and hid her caste for most of her life [1][2]. She has said that reading the last letter of the student Rohith Vemula made her stop hiding, and she started an online space, Documents of Dalit Discrimination, where Dalits could share their experiences [2][3]. Her memoir Coming Out as Dalit discusses Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and how caste affects areas from entertainment to the courts, and it won the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar, an Indian award for young writers, in 2020 [1][4]. Now based in Brooklyn, she has written for the New York Times and The Atlantic, and her writing helped shape Seattle's law against caste discrimination [5]. In April 2024 one of her US book talks, in Chicago, opened by celebrating Ambedkar's life to mark Ambedkar Jayanti and Dalit History Month [3].

name: Ambedkar Students' Association (ASA)
work: Student organisation at the University of Hyderabad that supports Dalit students and campaigns against caste discrimination on campus.
story: The Ambedkar Students' Association began at the University of Hyderabad in the early 1990s; The Caravan dates its start to 14 April 1994, Ambedkar's birthday, as a group devoted to the welfare of Dalit students [1]. Its first work was practical: helping Dalit students with admissions and fellowships, protecting them from ragging and making hostels and mess halls fairer [1]. Rohith Vemula, the Dalit scholar whose death in 2016 led to protests across India, was a member [1][2]. The group grew into a major force in campus politics, and in 2023 an alliance it was part of won the university's students' union election [2]. In January 2026 it organised the tenth-anniversary event where a people's draft of the Rohith Act, a proposed law against caste discrimination in higher education, was unveiled [3].

name: Anoop Kumar
work: Runs Nalanda Academy in Wardha, which helps students from marginalised communities reach top universities, after years of running a Dalit students' helpline.
story: Anoop Kumar, originally from Uttar Pradesh, fought caste discrimination as an engineering student in the late 1990s and later studied at JNU in Delhi [1]. With others, he ran a helpline for Dalit and Adivasi students for four years, and the group looked into 22 student suicides on campuses, turning what they found into documentaries called Death of Merit [1]. In 2013 he started Nalanda Academy in Wardha, Maharashtra, which has helped hundreds of students from marginalised castes enter leading universities in India and abroad [2][1]. He asks students who reach top campuses to go back and guide younger students in small towns and villages [1].

name: Bhim Army (Bhim Pathshalas)
work: Free, volunteer-run village schools started by the Bhim Army in western Uttar Pradesh to support Dalit children's education.
story: The Bhim Army, an Ambedkarite group from Saharanpur, Uttar Pradesh, founded by Chandrashekhar Azad and fellow activists, opened its first free school in 2015 [1][2]. The Bhim Pathshalas began as two-hour coaching classes after regular school, because many village government schools lacked basic facilities and Dalit families could not afford private schools [1][2]. Educated members teach for free, usually in a member's home, with members pooling money and materials [1][2]. Along with science and maths, children learn Dalit history and the lives of figures such as Ambedkar [1]. Estimates in 2018 ranged from about 350 to more than a thousand schools across districts such as Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Shamli and Meerut, and the classes went on even while Azad was jailed [1][2][3].

name: Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association (BAPSA)
work: Ambedkarite student group at JNU that brings together Dalit, Adivasi, backward-caste and minority students around anti-caste politics.
story: BAPSA was formed at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi in 2014 on the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda, the Adivasi freedom fighter [1]. Its name joins three icons — Birsa Munda, Ambedkar and Jotirao Phule — and it calls itself Ambedkarite, aiming to unite Dalit and other socially marginalised students [2]. Starting from a small base of votes, it grew into a serious contender in JNU's student elections [2][3]. In 2024 its candidate Priyanshi Arya was elected general secretary of the JNU students' union, the group's first win on the union's central panel [3]. Former members such as the rapper Sumeet Samos credit it with breaking the silence about caste on campus [4].

name: Raju Kendre
work: Founded the Eklavya India Foundation, which guides first-generation students from marginalised communities into higher education.
story: Raju Kendre grew up in a nomadic tribal community in Maharashtra and was the first in his family to go to university [1][3]. In 2017 he founded the Eklavya India Foundation to help students from marginalised communities become the first in their families to study at university [1]. The foundation raises awareness of university and scholarship options and runs mentoring, workshops and bootcamps in rural and tribal areas, in person and online [1]. In 2021 he won a Chevening Scholarship to study development studies at SOAS, University of London, and he has been featured in Forbes 30 Under 30 and named an Ashoka Fellow [1][2]. The foundation aims to reach 20,000 first-generation students and their families by 2030 [1].

name: Bezwada Wilson
work: Leads the Safai Karmachari Andolan, a national movement to end manual scavenging and to help the families trapped in it rebuild their lives.
story: Wilson was born in Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka, into a Dalit family that had done manual scavenging — cleaning human waste by hand — for generations, and he was the first in his family to go to college [1]. In 1986 he complained about the dry latrines in his town, first to local officials and then to the Prime Minister, and the latrines were rebuilt so that no one had to clean them by hand [1]. He went on to lead the Safai Karmachari Andolan, a community-driven movement, and in 2003 he and many other groups asked the Supreme Court to make governments enforce the 1993 law banning manual scavenging [1][2]. In 2016 he received the Ramon Magsaysay Award, often called Asia's Nobel Prize, for leading a grassroots movement to end this degrading work [2][3]. He came across Ambedkar's writings in 1990, and he describes his campaign as a fight to restore the dignity promised by the Constitution [1][4].

name: Kanshi Ram
work: Organised Dalit and backward-caste employees and voters across India through BAMCEF, DS4 and the Bahujan Samaj Party.
story: Kanshi Ram was born in 1934 in Ropar district, Punjab, and in 1957 joined a defence research laboratory near Pune as an assistant scientist [1]. When the lab cancelled holidays for Ambedkar Jayanti and Buddha Jayanti he protested, and reading Ambedkar's Annihilation of Caste deepened his commitment [1]. In 1978 he founded BAMCEF, a federation of educated employees from backward and minority communities, and in 1981 the DS4, a social organisation to rally Dalits and other exploited groups [1]. He travelled across the country by bicycle to understand people's lives, often speaking of the power of two wheels and two legs, and in 1984 he founded the Bahujan Samaj Party [1][2]. He died in 2006 [1].

name: Martin Macwan
work: Founded Navsarjan Trust and helped build the Dalit Shakti Kendra to fight untouchability and train young Dalits in skills and in using their rights.
story: Martin Macwan began social work as a student in Ahmedabad, joining his professors on a village survey at the age of 20 [1]. After four of his colleagues in a Dalit movement were killed by landlords in 1986, he founded Navsarjan in 1989 to fight untouchability, mainly in Gujarat [1]. He also helped run the Dalit Shakti Kendra, a vocational school that has trained about 11,000 young people in trades and in practical skills such as filing a police complaint and reading land records [1]. He received the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights Award in 2000 and also founded the Dalit Foundation [1]. When the government cancelled Navsarjan's licence to receive foreign funds and staff had to be let go, Macwan returned to lead it in 2016 [1][2].

name: Disha Wadekar
work: Supreme Court lawyer who takes up anti-discrimination and reservation cases and works to make India's legal profession more diverse.
story: Disha Wadekar trained as an engineer before studying law at Savitribai Phule Pune University, and she now practises before the Supreme Court and several High Courts [1]. Her work focuses on constitutional and anti-discrimination law for marginalised communities, and she has worked on major constitution bench cases, including the Sabarimala temple entry case and the challenge to reservations for the economically weaker sections [1][2]. In 2021 she co-founded the Community for the Eradication of Discrimination in Education and Employment (CEDE), which works for a more diverse legal profession and judiciary [1]. She has taught courses on law and marginalisation and sits on an academic committee on Denotified Tribes, communities once branded criminal under colonial law [1].

name: Paul Divakar Namala
work: Co-founded the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights and now links Dalits with other communities around the world who face discrimination because of birth or work.
story: Paul Divakar grew up in a Dalit family that was attacked for claiming its rights, including to public land, and his mother was killed in a petrol-bomb attack when he was 21 [1]. In 1998 he co-founded the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights (NCDHR) with leaders from across India, to record caste violence and raise it at home and abroad [1]. NCDHR documents abuses, gives legal help to victims and speaks up at the United Nations, and when it won Norway's Rafto Prize in 2007, Divakar was among those who received it [2]. In 2001 he was part of the Dalit team that pushed for caste to be discussed at the UN World Conference Against Racism in Durban [1]. Today he convenes a global forum of communities, such as Dalits and Roma, who face discrimination because of descent or work [1].

name: Radhika Vemula
work: Campaigns for a Rohith Act, a law to stop caste discrimination against students in colleges and universities.
story: Radhika Vemula is the mother of Rohith Vemula, a Dalit research scholar at the University of Hyderabad who was suspended and died by suicide in January 2016 [1]. Since then she has travelled widely and spoken to large crowds, asking that no other student should suffer what her son did [1]. She has pressed governments to pass a Rohith Act, a law against caste discrimination in higher education, comparing it to a vaccine against the disease of casteism [2]. On the tenth anniversary of his death, in January 2026, she helped unveil a people's draft of the law at the University of Hyderabad and met Telangana's Deputy Chief Minister to urge the state to pass it [2].

name: Anand Teltumbde
work: Scholar and writer on caste and class whose 2024 biography Iconoclast presents Ambedkar as a thinker to argue with, not an idol.
story: Anand Teltumbde is a scholar, writer and civil rights activist known for his books on caste, class and Dalit politics [1][3]. He was jailed under an anti-terror law in the Bhima Koregaon–Elgar Parishad case and spent 949 days in prison before the Bombay High Court granted him bail in November 2022 [1]. The court found no prima facie case against him, meaning the evidence did not even appear to support the charges at first look, and his was the first bail among the accused to be granted on merits [2]. While in prison he worked on Iconoclast: A Reflective Biography of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar, published by Penguin in 2024, which shows Ambedkar as a real person shaped by his times [3][4]. Reviewers note that he is willing to say where he thinks Ambedkar was wrong, treating Ambedkar's ideas as tools for thinking rather than objects of worship [4][5].

name: Ashok Gopal
work: Journalist and historian whose ten years of research produced A Part Apart, a detailed biography of Ambedkar that draws on Marathi sources.
story: Ashok Gopal is a journalist and historian who has also worked on designing school curricula [1]. He spent about ten years researching A Part Apart: The Life and Thought of B.R. Ambedkar, an 864-page biography published by Navayana in 2023 [2][3]. Unlike many English biographies, it draws deeply on Marathi material, including Changdev Khairmode's 12-volume Marathi biography of Ambedkar, the work of Vasant Moon and periodicals such as Janata, a paper Ambedkar ran [3][1]. The book won the New India Foundation's Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Book Prize in 2024, and Marathi, Tamil and Hindi editions were planned [2]. His publishers noted that until the book came out he could hardly be found on the internet — a sign of how quietly he had worked [2].

name: Bhagwan Das
work: Compiled Thus Spoke Ambedkar, a four-volume collection of Ambedkar's speeches, and took the issue of untouchability to the United Nations.
story: Bhagwan Das was born in 1927 into a sweeper community and faced caste discrimination from his teachers from the age of four [1]. As a teenager in Shimla in 1943 he met Ambedkar, and after serving in the air force during the Second World War he worked as a research assistant to Ambedkar in his last years [2][1]. In the years after Ambedkar's death he began collecting and editing his speeches into the four-volume Thus Spoke Ambedkar, giving readers a handy record of what Ambedkar said in public [2][3]. In 1983 he spoke about untouchability before a UN human rights body in Geneva, backed by a coalition of Dalit groups [2]. He became a Buddhist in 1957, wrote the memoir In Pursuit of Ambedkar, and died in November 2010 [1][2].

name: Gopal Guru
work: Political thinker who studies humiliation and self-respect in Dalit life, and edited the Economic and Political Weekly from 2018.
story: Gopal Guru is a political scientist who taught at the University of Pune, the University of Delhi and Jawaharlal Nehru University [1]. He is best known for his work on humiliation — the way caste attacks people's self-respect — and he edited a book of essays on the subject that discusses thinkers from Rousseau and Kant to Gandhi and Ambedkar [2]. He has argued that the insult Dalits face is a political question and should not be shrunk into a matter of hurt feelings [3]. In January 2018 he was appointed editor of the Economic and Political Weekly, one of India's leading journals of research and debate [1][4].

name: Hari Narke
work: Researcher who edited later volumes of Ambedkar's collected writings and brought the works of Phule and Ambedkar to wider readers.
story: Hari Narke (also spelled Narake) was born in 1963 into a poor family; his mother was a manual labourer, and he started out as a factory worker at TELCO in Pune [1]. While still in his teens he began researching and defending the ideas of Phule, Shahu Maharaj and Ambedkar, and he went on to write about 56 books, some translated into Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu [1]. He worked on the official English series of Ambedkar's writings and speeches, which library records list as compiled by Vasant Moon and edited by Narke [2]. He also headed the Mahatma Phule chair at Pune University and edited the works of Jotirao and Savitribai Phule [3][1]. He died in August 2023 at the age of 60, and leaders across Maharashtra's political parties paid tribute to his work [3].

work: Political scientist and writer who looks at Indian society from the viewpoint of the working castes that produce its food and goods.
story: Kancha Ilaiah was born in 1952 in a village in Warangal district, Telangana, into a Kurumaa shepherd family, and he later added Shepherd to his name to honour that identity [1][2]. His mother, who led about 25 shepherd families, was a strong early influence on his questioning of injustice [1]. He studied up to a doctorate at Osmania University in Hyderabad and taught political science there [1][2]. His 1996 book Why I Am Not a Hindu, written from the viewpoint of Shudra and Dalit communities — the working castes placed lowest in the old caste order — made him widely known and is now in its third edition [3]. He uses the word Dalitbahujan for Scheduled Castes and Other Backward Classes together and often speaks in public about Ambedkar and affirmative action [1].

name: Narendra Jadhav
work: Economist and writer whose bestselling family memoir and many books on Ambedkar have reached readers in more than a dozen languages.
story: Narendra Jadhav worked for 31 years at the Reserve Bank of India, rising to principal adviser and chief economist, and writes in English, Marathi and Hindi [1]. His 1993 Marathi book Aamcha Baap Aan Amhi tells the story of his Dalit parents; his father began to question the caste system partly inspired by Ambedkar's leadership [1][2]. The book has gone through 199 editions and has been translated into many Indian and foreign languages, including as Untouchables in English [1][3]. He has written 21 books on Ambedkar, among them Ambedkar: Awakening India's Social Conscience and Ambedkar: An Economist Extraordinaire (2016) [1][4]. He also served as vice-chancellor of the University of Pune from 2006, as a member of the Planning Commission from 2009 to 2014, and was nominated to the Rajya Sabha in 2016 [1][5].

name: Sukhadeo Thorat
work: Economist who uses data to measure caste discrimination and has shaped higher education policy, including as chairman of the University Grants Commission.
story: Sukhadeo Thorat is an economist who joined the faculty of Jawaharlal Nehru University in 1980 and is now a professor emeritus there [1]. His research uses surveys and numbers to show how untouchability and exclusion still shape Dalit lives, and he has written a book on Ambedkar's own role in economic planning and water policy [1]. He directed the Indian Institute of Dalit Studies in New Delhi from 2003 to 2006, chaired the University Grants Commission, which oversees India's universities, from 2006 to 2011, and later chaired the Indian Council of Social Science Research [1]. He has spoken often about how Dalit students are left out on campuses [2]. He received the Padma Shri in 2008 [1].

name: Vasant Moon
work: Compiled and edited the official English volumes of Ambedkar's writings and speeches for the Government of Maharashtra.
story: Vasant Moon (1932–2002) was a civil servant, writer and social activist who wrote in Marathi and English on social issues and Buddhism [1]. The Government of Maharashtra appointed him chief editor for compiling and editing Ambedkar's writings and speeches, and library records list the series as compiled by him [1][2]. This patient desk work means Ambedkar's own words are kept in libraries and free online collections such as the People's Archive of Rural India [3]. Moon also wrote a Marathi memoir of growing up among Dalits from the 1930s to the 1950s, the years of Ambedkar's movement [4]. Its English translation, Growing Up Untouchable in India, was hailed as the first book of its kind published in English and includes an account of Ambedkar and of Dalits turning to Buddhism [5].

name: Ashok Das
work: Founded Dalit Dastak, a Hindi magazine that grew into a YouTube channel and publishing house telling stories of Dalit achievement and struggle.
story: Ashok Das trained at the Indian Institute of Mass Communication and began working as a journalist in 2006 [1]. Having seen caste bias among people working in the media, he launched Dalit Dastak, a Hindi monthly magazine, in June 2012 [2][1][3]. He added a publishing house, Das Publications, in 2015 and a Dalit Dastak YouTube channel in 2017, which has more than 12 lakh (1.2 million) subscribers [1]. Rising printing costs forced the print magazine to stop in 2022, but the channel and the publishing work continue [1]. His focus on Dalit heroes and achievements, often missing from mainstream news, helps readers see their own history with pride [1].

name: Lahori Ram Balley (L.R. Balley)
work: Ran Bheem Patrika, described as the longest-running Ambedkarite magazine, and set up the Ambedkar Bhawan Trust in Jalandhar.
story: As a young man in Punjab, Lahori Ram Balley promised Ambedkar in September 1956, when Ambedkar was gravely ill, that he would spend the rest of his life spreading his mission [1]. He resigned from his government job on 6 December 1956, the day of Ambedkar's death, to keep that promise [1]. He was a founder of Bheem Patrika, published since 1958 and described as the longest-running Ambedkarite magazine [1]. In 1972 he set up the Ambedkar Bhawan Trust in Jalandhar, and he was also a member of the Samata Sainik Dal, a volunteer body Ambedkar had founded [1]. He kept that 1956 promise for more than six decades and died at his home in Jalandhar in July 2023, aged 93 [1].

name: Meena Kotwal
work: Founded The Mooknayak, a reader-funded news site in Hindi and English that reports on Dalit, Adivasi and other marginalised communities.
story: Meena Kotwal grew up in Delhi as the daughter of labourers, studied mass media at Jamia Millia Islamia and joined BBC Hindi in 2017 [1]. She filed a complaint of caste discrimination there, which the BBC's internal inquiry did not uphold, and she decided to build a newsroom of her own [1]. In January 2021 she started The Mooknayak with her savings, naming it after the paper Ambedkar launched in 1920 to speak for people whose voices went unheard [1]. The site publishes in Hindi and English, refuses advertising and political party money, and survives on crowdfunding from readers [1][2]. Its reporting has pushed officials to act in several cases, such as bringing electricity to a village, even as Kotwal has faced threats and online abuse that UN experts raised with the government [1].

name: Raees Muhammad (Ravichandran Bathran)
work: Started Dalit Camera, a volunteer-run YouTube channel that records Dalit voices, protests and testimonies that mainstream media often ignore.
story: Ravichandran Bathran, the first Dalit from his home area in Tamil Nadu to go to college, began filming in 2011 while studying at the English and Foreign Languages University in Hyderabad [1][2][3]. Frustrated that the news rarely covered Dalit lives, he set up the YouTube channel Dalit Camera with the tagline Through Untouchable Eyes [1][3]. A small team, mostly volunteers travelling by bus on tiny budgets, recorded interviews and testimonies about caste violence and discrimination on campuses [1]. After Rohith Vemula's death in 2016 the channel documented student protests and interviews with academics and students [2]. In 2020 he converted to Islam and took the name Raees Muhammad, keeping his old name as part of his identity; he now runs a sanitation business in the Nilgiris and plans to revive the channel [3].

name: Round Table India
work: An online magazine and library that publishes news, essays and creative writing from a Dalit-Bahujan point of view.
story: Round Table India is a news and opinion website that looks at society, politics and policy from a Dalit-Bahujan viewpoint — Bahujan means the majority made up of oppressed communities [1]. Its own About page names its founders as Bhanu Pratap Singh, Anu Ramdas and Kuffir (Naren Bedide), with Anu Ramdas and Kuffir as editors [2]. It has been online since around 2009 and gives space to students, writers, scholars and activists whose voices rarely appear in mainstream media [3]. Besides commentary, it keeps a library of writings by thinkers such as Ambedkar and Phule and material on Dalit history and movements [1]. Its tagline calls for an informed Ambedkar age [1].

name: Yogesh Maitreya
work: Poet, translator and founder of Panther's Paw Publication, a small press that publishes Dalit writers in English and in translation.
story: Yogesh Maitreya started Panther's Paw Publication in 2016 from his hostel room while working on a PhD at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences in Mumbai [1]. The press, based in Nagpur, publishes anti-caste stories by Dalit authors — original English writing as well as translations from four Indian languages — and has paid for its books through crowdfunding [1]. Its books include the memoir of rapper Sumeet Samos, Affairs of Caste [2]. Maitreya is also a writer himself, and his books include Flowers on the Grave of Caste, a collection of short stories [3].

name: Arivu (Arivarasu Kalainesan)
work: Tamil rapper and lyricist whose songs retell Ambedkar's life and challenge caste, from Jaibhim Thalaimurai to Enjoy Enjaami.
story: Arivarasu Kalainesan, known as Arivu, is from Arakkonam near Chennai; his parents, a college professor and a government schoolteacher, both took part in a Tamil Nadu literacy movement [1]. He studied mechanical engineering, then joined The Casteless Collective, the anti-caste band formed with Pa. Ranjith's support, and wrote lyrics drawing on Ambedkar's ideas for the 2018 film Kaala [1][2]. In 2020 he released Jaibhim Thalaimurai, a rap that traces Ambedkar's life, his struggles and his embrace of Buddhism in 1956 [2]. His lyrics for Enjoy Enjaami, a song about roots and equality, neared 200 million YouTube views by 2021 [1][3]. When he was left out of credit for that song, many saw it as part of a wider pattern of erasing Dalit artists, and he spoke up to claim his work [4].

name: Ginni Mahi
work: Punjabi folk and rap singer whose songs celebrate Ambedkar and Guru Ravidas and turn caste insults into pride.
story: Ginni Mahi, born Gurkanwal Bharti, comes from a Ravidassia family in Punjab — a community that follows the teachings of the poet-saint Guru Ravidas — and began singing at functions from the age of 13 [1]. When a fan asked her caste and then warned her that Chamars (a Dalit community whose name was long used as an insult) are dangerous, she replied with a song, Danger Chamar, calling on the community to unite against inequality [1]. The song went viral, and she has also sung in praise of Ambedkar and against female foeticide, the killing of unborn girls [1][2]. She calls Ravidas and Ambedkar her two gurus and sings about equality, human values and the Constitution [1]. As a teenager she was already being described as a Punjabi pop sensation who brought Dalit pride into popular music [3].

name: Meena Kandasamy
work: Poet, novelist and translator whose writing exposes caste violence and patriarchy and carries Tamil anti-caste thought to readers worldwide.
story: Meena Kandasamy, born in 1984, is a poet, novelist and translator based in Chennai [1]. As a young woman she edited The Dalit, an English magazine of the Dalit Media Network, in 2001–02, and worked with the Dalit Panthers of India, a Dalit political movement [1]. She translated the speeches of Dalit leader Thol. Thirumavalavan into English, and her first poetry collection, Touch, came out in 2006 [1]. Her novel The Gypsy Goddess retells the 1968 Kilvenmani massacre, in which landless Dalit farm workers and their families were killed in Tamil Nadu [2][3]. Her books are published and read well beyond India [2][3].

name: Neeraj Ghaywan
work: Film director who speaks openly about his Dalit identity and tells stories of caste, friendship and dignity, from Masaan to Homebound.
story: Neeraj Ghaywan was born in Hyderabad, studied engineering and business, and left a corporate job to work as an assistant on the film Gangs of Wasseypur [1]. For much of his life he hid his Dalit identity, even changing his surname to Kumar, but he began to speak openly about it after his first film, Masaan, was praised at Cannes in 2015 [1]. His later work, including the short films Geeli Pucchi and Juice, keeps returning to how caste overlaps with gender and class [2]. His 2025 film Homebound, about two childhood friends, received a long standing ovation at Cannes and was chosen as India's official entry for the Academy Awards [1][3]. He has pointed out that very few Indian films tell Dalit stories and that most of them were made by people from privileged castes [4].

name: Pa. Ranjith
work: Film director and producer who puts Dalit lives at the centre of popular Tamil cinema and runs the Neelam cultural organisation.
story: Pa. Ranjith grew up in Karapakkam near Avadi, on the edge of Chennai, studied fine arts, and made his first film, Attakathi, in 2012 [1]. His later films, including Madras and the Rajinikanth films Kabali and Kaala, brought caste oppression and the lives of marginalised people into mainstream Tamil cinema, and he calls himself an Ambedkarite [1]. Through his Neelam organisation he produces other filmmakers' work, holds music festivals and workshops, and runs a night school in Dharmapuri decorated with images of Ambedkar, the Buddha and Tamil anti-caste leaders [1][2][3]. Neelam Cultural Centre also helped form The Casteless Collective, a band that mixes gaana — Chennai's street music — with rap and has released songs honouring Ambedkar [1][4][5]. He rejects being boxed in as only a Dalit filmmaker and says that for him everything is political [1][6].

work: Anti-caste rapper and writer from Odisha who raps in English, Hindi and Odia about caste and dignity.
story: Sumeet Samos grew up in Tentulipadar village in Koraput, Odisha, in the Dom community, a Scheduled Caste [1]. At Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi he was active in the Birsa Ambedkar Phule Students' Association, which helped break the silence about caste on campus [1][2]. His rap songs, such as Ladai Seekh Le (Learn to Fight), urge young people to stand up to caste injustice [3][4]. Turned down for scholarships, he raised the money for a master's degree at Oxford University through crowdfunding [5]. His memoir Affairs of Caste, shaped by Ambedkarite thought, traces his journey from Koraput to JNU and Oxford [1].

name: Chandra Bhan Prasad
work: Writer and thinker who champions Dalit capitalism and the learning of English as paths out of caste-bound work.
story: Chandra Bhan Prasad, who studied international affairs at JNU, began writing the weekly Dalit Diary column in The Pioneer in 1999, becoming the first Dalit with a regular column in a national English newspaper [1]. He is known for the idea of Dalit capitalism — the belief that Dalits can gain power by owning businesses — and his 2002 Bhopal Document for the Madhya Pradesh government set out that agenda [2]. In 2010 he unveiled a statue of a Goddess English at a school in Lakhimpur Kheri, Uttar Pradesh, a symbol meant to make Dalit children less afraid of learning English; officials later shut the small temple down [3][4]. He has also worked alongside Milind Kamble to speak about the rise of Dalit entrepreneurs [5].

name: Kalpana Saroj
work: Dalit businesswoman who rose from child marriage and poverty to revive the debt-ridden Kamani Tubes company.
story: Kalpana Saroj grew up near Akola in Maharashtra, the daughter of a police constable, and was married at about 12 to a much older man [1]. After leaving the marriage she moved to Mumbai as a teenager and worked as a tailor in a hosiery company [1]. With a Rs 50,000 bank loan from a government scheme for Scheduled Castes named after Mahatma Phule, she started a furniture business in Ulhasnagar [1]. In 2006 she became chairperson of Kamani Tubes, a failing company buried in debt, and led its revival [1][2]. She received the Padma Shri in 2013 [2][3].

name: Milind Kamble
work: Founded the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry to help Dalits become business owners and job creators.
story: Milind Kamble, a civil engineer and entrepreneur, founded the Dalit Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DICCI) in Pune in 2005 [1]. It was the first Indian business association set up to promote entrepreneurship among Dalits [2]. DICCI has grown to 29 state chapters and 7 international chapters, with members in fields from chemicals, textiles and solar energy to healthcare, hospitality and trade [1]. Kamble received the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, in 2013 [2].

name: Shanti Swaroop Bauddh
work: Built Samyak Prakashan in Delhi, which published more than 2,000 books on Buddhism and Ambedkar's thought, mostly in Hindi.
story: Shanti Swaroop Bauddh grew up in Delhi in a family close to the Ambedkarite movement; his grandfather worked with Ambedkar, who is said to have suggested the boy's name [1]. He built Samyak Prakashan, a Delhi publishing house for Buddhist and Ambedkarite literature, which brought out more than 2,000 books, many translated into other languages [1]. He followed Ambedkar's call to embrace Buddhism closely and worked to strengthen the Buddhist movement in India, speaking at gatherings such as a memorial meeting at a Buddha Vihar in north Delhi [1]. His books also presented saints such as Ravidas and Kabir as carrying Buddhist ideas, and he tried to connect Ambedkarites around the world [1]. He died on 6 June 2020 [1][2].

name: Asha Kowtal
work: Led the All India Dalit Mahila Adhikar Manch, a Dalit women's movement that records caste and gender violence and trains women leaders.
story: Asha Kowtal served as general secretary of the All India Dalit Mahila Adhikar Manch (AIDMAM), whose name means All India Dalit Women's Rights Forum [1][2]. The forum grew out of the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights because Dalit women felt they needed their own movement to face both caste and male dominance [1]. It runs leadership training and legal education, and its members visit villages to record violence against Dalit women [1]. Starting with a march in Haryana in 2012, AIDMAM held self-respect yatras — long journeys through states such as Haryana, Bihar and Odisha — and in 2015 it toured North America to speak about caste-based sexual violence [1].

name: Ruth Manorama
work: Builds organisations that help Dalit women and slum dwellers claim their rights, and leads the National Federation of Dalit Women.
story: Ruth Manorama was born in Chennai in 1952 to a Dalit family and trained as a social worker at the University of Madras [1]. In 1985 she started Women's Voice, which works with women in city slums on land, housing and survival rights, and she led protests and court cases against the demolition of slum homes in Karnataka [1]. She is president of the National Federation of Dalit Women, set up in 1995 as a platform for Dalit women across India, and of the National Alliance of Women, which checks whether the government keeps its promises to women [1]. In 2006 she received the Right Livelihood Award for decades of work for the equality of Dalit women at home and abroad [1]. At the UN Human Rights Council she has argued that Dalit women are not only victims but agents of change [2].

name: Beena Pallical
work: Checks how much of India's national budget truly reaches Dalits and Adivasis, as general secretary of the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights.
story: Beena Pallical is general secretary of the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights (NCDHR) and one of its main voices on public budgets [1][2]. Each year NCDHR studies the Union Budget to see how much of the money marked for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes goes to schemes that directly help them [1][2]. In 2021, for example, its analysis found that only 52 of 330 schemes listed for Scheduled Castes were actually targeted at them, and that money for post-matric scholarships fell short of student demand [1]. She has argued that funds for Dalit and Adivasi women are especially thin [2].

name: P.S. Krishnan
work: Civil servant who spent six decades writing laws and policies for Dalits and backward classes, including the 1989 law against atrocities.
story: P.S. Krishnan, an upper-caste Hindu from Kerala, joined the Indian Administrative Service in 1957 and in his first posting camped in a Dalit settlement that upper-caste villagers had never entered [1]. He wrote the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989, a law that punishes violence and humiliation aimed at Dalits and Adivasis [1][2]. In 1990 he wrote the cabinet note that led to reservations for Other Backward Classes under the Mandal Commission report, and he helped draft the 1993 law banning manual scavenging [1]. After retiring he served the National Commission for Backward Classes and kept pressing for land for landless Dalits until his death in 2019 [1]. He also helped plan the national celebrations of Ambedkar's birth centenary [3].

name: Bojja Tharakam
work: Human rights lawyer and poet who fought the court cases of Dalit massacre survivors in Andhra Pradesh and taught ordinary people their legal rights.
story: Bojja Tharakam was born in a hamlet in the Konaseema area of East Godavari district, and in the 1960s he helped start the Ambedkar Yuvajana Sangham, a youth group inspired by Babasaheb [1]. He gave up his post as a government lawyer in protest after the Karamchedu massacre of Dalits, then helped the survivors organise, rebuild their lives and fight their court cases [1]. He founded the Dalit Mahasabha and took up the cases of the Tsundur and Lakshmipeta massacres, cases that few other lawyers wanted [1]. His small Telugu book on what to do if the police arrest you sold lakhs of copies, and his book Kulam-Vargam explained how he joined Ambedkar's ideas with Marxist thought [1]. He died in September 2016 after a long fight with a brain tumour [1][2].

name: Dona Biswas
work: Ambedkarite reporter at EastMojo who writes about how caste and the lives of Dalits are overlooked in Assam.
story: Dona Biswas is a reporter for EastMojo, a news site that covers North-East India, where she is described as an Ambedkarite scholar from Assam [1][3]. In January 2025 she and Sanjana Hazarika wrote about an Ambedkarite book stall that the Assam unit of the All India Independent Scheduled Castes Association (AIISCA) set up at the Assam Book Fair in Guwahati [1]. Their article noted that Scheduled Caste communities, the official term for groups that faced untouchability, make up 7.15% of Assam's people, yet the state has not had a well-organised Dalit movement [1]. In June 2025 she wrote, as a Dalit from Assam, about visiting the Ambedkar Bhawan at Uzanbazar in Guwahati, finding it neglected, and doubting official promises such as a planned Ambedkar statue [2]. In April 2026 EastMojo published her piece asking whether Ambedkar Jayanti exposes Assam's silence on caste and politics [3].

name: Budh Sharan Hans
work: Retired Bihar civil servant who has published the advertisement-free magazine Ambedkar Mission since 1993 and sends bags of books to villages.
story: Budh Sharan Hans was born in 1942 into a poor Paswan Dalit family in Tilora village of Gaya district, and he served in the Bihar State Administrative Service from 1969 to 2000 [1][2]. He embraced Buddhism in 1978 at Bodh Gaya and took a new name that honours the Buddha [2]. In 1993 he started the magazine Ambedkar Mission, which grew from a quarterly into a monthly, carries no advertisements and reaches about 5,000 readers in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states [2]. He also runs a publishing house of the same name and has written short stories, five volumes of autobiography and dozens of booklets spreading the ideas of Phule and Ambedkar [1][2]. Through his Savitribai Jhola Pustakalaya, a book-bag library, he has given out more than 500 bags of books, and he planned to turn later volumes of Ambedkar's writings into simple booklets for villagers [2].

name: Anita Bharti
work: Award-winning Delhi government school principal and Hindi Dalit feminist writer whose poems and stories carry Ambedkar's vision.
story: Anita Bharti was born in Delhi in 1965 and has built a career in government schools, becoming principal of the Government Senior Secondary School in Roopnagar, New Delhi [1][2]. Her honours include the Radhakrishnan Teacher Award, a Delhi State Teacher's honour and several Savitribai Phule awards [1][3]. In her book Samkaleen Narivad aur Dalit Stree ka Pratirodh she argues, from the standpoint of Dalit women, against a feminism led by upper castes [2]. Her poems, including one that pictures Ambedkar living on in everyone who follows his path, keep Babasaheb's vision at the centre of her writing [2]. Nikhil Pandhi's English translation of her stories, Chronicle of the Quota Woman and Other Stories, was chosen for an English PEN translation award [1][2].

name: Rajni Tilak
work: Delhi Dalit feminist, poet and organiser who pushed the Dalit and women's movements to face caste and patriarchy together.
story: Rajni Tilak was the eldest of seven children in a Delhi family of limited means, and she gave up higher studies to help raise her siblings, training instead at an industrial training institute [1]. While there she began organising girls from marginalised families, and she later helped mobilise thousands of anganwadi (village childcare centre) workers to demand fair pay [1]. She worked with the Dalit Panthers, the Dalit Lekhak Sangh, the National Federation of Dalit Women and other groups, drawing on Ambedkar's ideas [1][2]. She challenged the Left and the women's movement to take caste seriously, and the Dalit movement to face its own patriarchy [1]. She marked Savitribai Phule's birthday as Education Day, edited Phule's collected works and an anthology of Dalit women's writing, and died on 30 March 2018 [1].

name: Manjula Pradeep
work: Dalit human rights lawyer from Gujarat who led Navsarjan Trust and now runs the WAYVE Foundation for marginalised women and young people.
story: Manjula Pradeep, a Dalit woman from Gujarat, joined the Dalit rights group Navsarjan Trust after a master's degree in social work and became its first woman employee [1]. She rose to become its executive director, training Dalit activists, giving legal aid, and pressing for land reform and an end to manual scavenging [1][2]. In 2008, as a lawyer, she took up the case of a young Dalit woman sexually abused by six of her college professors, after which Navsarjan took on more than 35 cases of sexual violence [1]. She later founded the WAYVE Foundation for marginalised youth and in 2021 co-founded the National Council of Women Leaders [2][3]. She has spent more than 15 years raising caste discrimination at the United Nations and the European Parliament, and the BBC named her among its 100 inspiring and influential women of 2021 [2][3].

name: Ravi Kumar Dalit
work: Shimla vegetable seller and Ambedkarite who keeps raising Dalit issues in Himachal Pradesh's capital.
story: Ravi Kumar Dalit earns his living by selling vegetables in Shimla, the capital of Himachal Pradesh [1]. Forward Press describes him as an Ambedkarite who is well known in the city for raising issues that affect Dalits while he runs his stall [1]. He has even contested an assembly election against Virbhadra Singh on a Bahujan Samaj Party ticket [1].

name: Devanur Mahadeva
work: Kannada writer and a founder of the Dalit Sangharsha Samiti, which organised Dalits across Karnataka for land, education and dignity.
story: Born in Devanuru in 1948, Devanur Mahadeva is one of the founding members of the Dalit Sangharsha Samiti (DSS), a movement that organised Dalits in Karnataka around land rights, education and a real say in democracy [1]. His novels Odalaala (1978) and Kusumabale (1988) brought Dalit life and speech into Kannada literature [1]. He won the Sahitya Akademi Award and the Padma Shri, and in 2015 he returned both to protest growing intolerance [1]. His 64-page Kannada booklet on the RSS sold more than three lakh copies, which shows how widely people read him [1]. In December 2024 the Tamil Nadu government gave him its Vaikom Award for social justice, and his thinking draws on Ambedkar along with Gandhi and Lohia [1][2].

name: Siddalingaiah
work: Kannada poet and co-founder of the Dalit Sangharsha Samiti whose protest songs were sung at Dalit gatherings across Karnataka.
story: Siddalingaiah, born in Magadi in 1954, was a co-founder of the Dalit Sangharsha Samiti and is credited with launching the Dalit-Bandaya (Dalit and rebel) movement that made Dalit writing a genre in Kannada [1][2]. One of his best-known songs asked who had really gained from India's independence in 1947 [1]. Pointing to Ambedkar's warnings in the Constituent Assembly, he argued that political freedom means little without freedom from caste-based social and economic bondage [1]. He headed the Kannada department at Bangalore University, served in both houses of the state legislature, chaired the Kannada Development Authority, received the Pampa Award and wrote the autobiography Ooru Keri [1][2]. He died in Bengaluru on 11 June 2021 of COVID-19 complications [1][2].

name: K.K. Kochu
work: Dalit historian and writer who retold Kerala's history from the side of its oppressed communities and wrote a Malayalam book on Ambedkar's life.
story: K.K. Kochu was born in Kallara in Kottayam district in 1949 and worked for the Kerala State Road Transport Corporation from 1977 to 2001 while he wrote and organised [1]. He helped build groups such as the People's Workers' Union and a Human Rights Committee [1]. His books include Kerala Charitravum Samooha Roopeekaranavum, a study of Kerala's history and society, and Ambedkar: Jeevithavum Dauthyavum, a Malayalam book on Ambedkar's life and mission [1][3]. His autobiography Dalitan tells the story of modern Kerala from the point of view of those pushed to the bottom, and it has been translated into English by Radhika P. Menon [1][2]. He received the Kerala Sahitya Akademi Award for his overall contribution and died in Kottayam on 13 March 2025 [1][2].

name: Sunny M. Kapicadu
work: Kerala Dalit thinker and speaker who joins protests by oppressed communities and argues for Ambedkar's ideas in public debate.
story: Sunny M. Kapicadu is described by the Ambedkarite web magazine Round Table India as one of Kerala's most prominent Dalit activists and intellectuals, and he has earned his living as an employee of the Life Insurance Corporation [1][2]. He has taken part in many protests by Dalits and other oppressed groups in Kerala [1][2]. In a 2015 speech in Ernakulam, he argued that the fight against fascism should draw on Ambedkar, who studied how caste power works, along with Kerala reformers Sree Narayana Guru and Ayyankali [1]. He calls himself an Ambedkarite and has said that Ambedkar's ideas remain deeply important in India [2]. Writers on Malayalam Dalit criticism count him among the activist-critics working on land and political rights [3].
