name: Ashif Shaikh
work: Founder of Jan Sahas, which helps women leave manual scavenging, rebuild their livelihoods and lead a campaign for dignity.
story: Ashif Shaikh was born into a Dalit Muslim family in Indore and faced caste discrimination and violence as a child [1]. In 1999 he formed a youth group that ran night classes and freed children from labour, and Jan Sahas, the organisation he went on to found, takes Ambedkar's call to educate, agitate and organise as its guiding principle [1][2]. Through its Rashtriya Garima Abhiyan (National Campaign for Dignity), Jan Sahas helps people forced to clean human waste by hand, most of them women, to quit this work and find new livelihoods such as tailoring [1][2]. Its Maila Mukti Yatra, a march against manual scavenging, covered 10,000 km with about 50,000 participants, and thousands of freed women burned the baskets they had once used to carry waste [2]. The Better India reported that Jan Sahas had rescued or rehabilitated close to 41,000 manual scavengers and bonded labourers, and it also trains survivors of sexual violence as barefoot paralegals [1].

name: Anand Shinde
work: Marathi singer of Bhim geet, songs that honour Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, from a family that has sung them across three generations.
story: Anand Shinde is a Marathi singer known for Bhim geet, songs that honour Dr. B.R. Ambedkar [1][3]. In 2016, Scroll named his song A for Ambedkar as one example of the Dalit music and hopes spreading across India [2]. A 2024 column in ThePrint remembered his songs, along with Kadubai Kharat's, playing over and over in one family's home on Ambedkar Jayanti, the yearly celebration of Ambedkar's birthday [3]. He belongs to a well-known singing family: Round Table India lists him with his father Prahlad Shinde, his brother Milind Shinde and his son Adarsh Shinde as one family line of Bhim song singers [1][5]. His son Adarsh has been described as carrying the family's Bhim geet tradition into its third generation [4].

name: J.V. Pawar
work: Co-founder of the Dalit Panthers who has spent decades writing the history of the Ambedkarite movement after Babasaheb.
story: J.V. Pawar co-founded the Dalit Panthers, the angry young Dalit movement of 1970s Maharashtra, and served as its general secretary [1][2]. A poet and novelist, he wrote the novel Balidaan (1969) and the poetry collection Naakebandi (1976), later published in English as Blockade [1]. He has written several volumes recording and analysing Dalit movements in the years after Ambedkar's death [1]. His first-hand history of the Panthers, written in Marathi, was published in English by Forward Press as Dalit Panthers: An Authoritative History [2]. He describes himself as a lifelong Ambedkarite [1].

name: Kadubai Kharat
work: Sings Bhim geet, songs that honour Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, while playing the one-stringed ektari, and has become well known across Maharashtra.
story: Kadubai Kharat grew up poor in Jalna district, Maharashtra, and was widowed young with three children; after her father died, she went door to door with his ektari, a one-stringed instrument, singing devotional songs for food [1]. Her life changed when a woman asked her to sing about Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and gave her about a month's food in return; she then took up Ambedkar's path and in 2016 gave up Hinduism and became a Buddhist [1]. One of her Bhim geet, songs that honour Ambedkar, went viral online, and she has sung on TV shows such as Jalsa Maharashtracha [1][2]. Writers on Ambedkarite culture name her among the best-known Bhim geet singers, and a 2024 column in ThePrint remembered her songs playing again and again at home on Ambedkar Jayanti, the yearly celebration of Ambedkar's birthday [3][4]. In 2023, PARI reported that she still lived in a small tin hut, with no water or electricity, beside the Aurangabad–Beed bypass road [1].

name: Sambhaji Bhagat
work: Shahir (people's balladeer) who sings Ambedkarite songs in villages and city settlements, turning Marathi folk forms into songs against caste.
story: Sambhaji Bhagat came to Mumbai in 1979 from Mahu, a village in Satara district, joined the street theatre group Avahan Natya Manch, and is now counted among Maharashtra's leading Ambedkarite shahirs [1][2]. He performs mostly in villages and slum settlements, turning Marathi folk forms such as the powada and bharud into songs about caste, the state and Dalit leadership [1]. He took part in the Namantar Andolan, the long campaign to rename Marathwada University after Dr. Ambedkar, and in 2004 he started his own troupe, the Vidrohi Shahiri Jalsa [1]. He calls himself an Ambedkarite, and his audiences often answer his songs with Jai Bhim [1]. He also composed and sang songs for the award-winning Marathi film Court and helped inspire one of its main characters [1].

name: Shahir Atmaram Salve
work: Marathwada shahir whose songs powered the Namantar movement to rename Marathwada University after Dr. Ambedkar.
story: Atmaram Salve was born in 1953 in Bhatwadgaon village in Beed district and came to Aurangabad as a student at Milind College, which Dr. Ambedkar had founded [1]. He used shahiri, Maharashtra's tradition of ballad singing, to drive the Namantar movement, the campaign to rename Marathwada University after Babasaheb, and he was a Marathwada vice-president of the Bharatiya Dalit Panthers [1]. He wrote more than 300 songs about equality and resistance to caste, and large crowds came to hear him in villages and Dalit settlements [1]. Police often shut down his programmes, he faced many criminal cases between 1978 and 1991, and he was even barred from entering Beed district [1]. He died in 1991, and PARI remembers him as a martyr of the movement [1].

name: Sheetal Sathe
work: Singer and poet who writes and performs shahiri songs about Babasaheb, caste and the lives of the poor with the troupe Navayan Mahajalsa.
story: Sheetal Sathe grew up hearing her family sing and joined the Pune cultural group Kabir Kala Manch after watching shahir Sambhaji Bhagat perform on Savitribai Phule's birth anniversary [1]. She began writing her own songs, many about Babasaheb and about rising prices, and they drew a strong response in bastis, the working-class settlements where she sang [1]. After the Khairlanji atrocity against a Dalit family, the group toured Maharashtra singing against caste [1]. In 2013 she was jailed while pregnant after the authorities accused the group of Maoist links, and the Bombay High Court released her on humanitarian grounds that June [1]. With her partner Sachin Mali she co-founded the shahiri troupe Navayan Mahajalsa, which the Goethe-Institut describes as being at the front of India's anti-caste cultural movement [1][2].

name: Suvarna Salve
work: Shahir with Samata Kala Manch who sings anti-caste songs with a dafli (hand drum) in working-class settlements.
story: Suvarna Salve was moved to act by caste atrocities and by a shahiri jalsa, an evening of protest songs, held by the Republican Panthers in Byculla, Mumbai [1]. She joined the group, which renamed itself Samata Kala Manch in 2017, and she sings shahiri songs with a dafli in bastis [1]. Her songs have taken up events such as the flogging of Dalits in Una, the disappearance of the student Najeeb Ahmed and the protests against the citizenship law [1]. She says Babasaheb is central to her life and that her thinking follows his vision and that of Jyotiba and Savitribai Phule [1]. She has kept going despite pushback from family and society, with her mother and sister supporting her [1].

name: Urmila Pawar
work: Marathi writer and activist whose memoir and stories bring Dalit women's lives, work and Ambedkarite awakening into literature.
story: Urmila Pawar grew up in a Mahar Dalit community on the Konkan coast, then moved to Mumbai, where she fought for Dalit rights and became a major voice in the Dalit literary movement [1]. She worked in a bank while studying for her degrees and raising her children [2]. Her memoir Aaydan (2003), published in English as The Weave of My Life, follows three generations of Dalit women [1][2]. The book describes how her community took up Ambedkar's ideas and embraced Buddhism, and the scholar Sharmila Rege called it a Dalit feminist testimony [2]. She writes in Marathi but is read across India [1].

name: Akhila Naik
work: College teacher of Odia literature in Kalahandi whose novel Bheda is described as the first Odia Dalit novel.
story: Akhila Naik teaches Odia literature at Government College, Bhawanipatna, in Odisha's Kalahandi district [1]. His novel Bheda, first serialised in the Odia magazine Paschima and published in 2010, is described as the first Odia Dalit novel [1][2]. It follows Laltu, the son of a Dalit school principal, who drops out of school and becomes an activist leading his people against caste oppression [1][2]. Its translator Raj Kumar says the hero is modelled on B.R. Ambedkar, and that Naik believes education must go hand in hand with political action [2]. Naik has written that he saw and lived through the novel's events himself, and Oxford University Press published it in English [1][2].

name: Balbir Madhopuri
work: Punjabi Dalit writer and translator whose autobiography Changiya Rukh tells of caste and child labour in a Punjab village.
story: Balbir Madhopuri began life as a child labourer and farm worker in the Punjab village of Madhopur, and he went on to earn a postgraduate degree in Punjabi from Lyallpur Khalsa College, Jalandhar [1][2]. His autobiography Chhangiya Rukh appeared in Punjabi in 2002, and Oxford University Press published it in English in 2010 as Changiya Rukh: Against the Night, with editions also in Hindi, Urdu, Russian and Polish [1][2]. His own books, which include the poetry collection My Caste-My Shadow and a book on Ghadri Baba Mangu Ram, focus on Dalits and other deprived people in a caste-based society [2]. He has also translated about 45 books and edited about 45 more in Punjabi [1]. After retiring in 2015 as a Deputy Director in the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, he directed Punjabi Bhawan in New Delhi and edited the quarterly Samkali Sahit [1][2].

name: Bhanwar Meghwanshi
work: Rajasthan writer, journalist and cultural activist who left the RSS over caste exclusion and now travels the state spreading Ambedkarite ideas.
story: Bhanwar Meghwanshi joined the RSS as a 13-year-old and stayed from 1987 to 1991, but he left after senior members refused to eat food cooked in his Dalit family's home [1]. He told this story in his Hindi memoir Main Ek Karsevak Tha (2019), later published in English as I Could Not Be Hindu [1][2]. After leaving, he turned to Ambedkar and became an Ambedkarite author and cultural activist who travels across Rajasthan to spread the movement [2][3]. On 14 January 2001 he started Diamond India, a publication for his Meghwal community [2][3]. He also took up the Dangawas case, in which Dalit farm workers who fought for land rights were killed, even when some groups opposed him for it [3].

name: Prabhati Lal (P.L.) Mimroth
work: Former railway employee turned lawyer who founded Jaipur's Centre for Dalit Rights and trained young lawyers to use the atrocities law.
story: P.L. Mimroth was born in 1939 in Biwai village in Dausa district, studied law at Delhi University, and worked for Northern Railways from 1959 until 1985 [1]. He then took early retirement to practise law for Dalit rights, arguing cases in the Delhi and Rajasthan High Courts [1]. After the 1992 Kumher massacre, in which 19 Dalits were burnt alive, he set up the Centre for Dalit Rights in Jaipur, which investigated attacks, supported victims through trials and won a fight against the denial of drinking water to Dalits in Chakwada [1][2]. He ran workshops on the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, built a network of young lawyers and was a founder member of the National Campaign on Dalit Human Rights [1]. Remembered as an Ambedkarite, he died on 24 February 2023 and donated his body to a medical college, as he had wished [1][2].

name: A. Kathir (Evidence Kathir)
work: Founder of Evidence, a Madurai rights group that investigates attacks on Dalits and campaigns for a law against killings in the name of family honour.
story: A. Kathir founded and directs Evidence, a Madurai-based human rights organisation that investigates violence against Dalits in Tamil Nadu [1][2]. By 2017 the group had spent about twelve years documenting such cases, recording around 150 to 180 a year and checking police charge sheets to see whether the accused had even been arrested [1]. Kathir visits villages after killings, and the group's reports, such as its finding that more than 25 Dalit activists were murdered in one year, are picked up by newspapers [1]. In 2022, as head of the Dalit Human Rights Defenders Network, he handed Chief Minister M.K. Stalin a draft law against crimes carried out in the name of family honour [2]. In March 2026 he and Kowsalya, a survivor of such an attack, gave a state commission data on 53 honour killing incidents between 2017 and 2025 [3].

name: J. Balasubramaniam
work: Writer and academic who tracks down and documents the forgotten Dalit and Ambedkarite journals of Tamil Nadu.
story: J. Balasubramaniam is a writer and academic who has spent years tracing old Dalit and Ambedkarite magazines printed in Tamil Nadu [1]. An earlier book of his documented more than 40 Dalit journals published between 1869 and 1943 [1]. His book Thamizhagathil Ambedkariya Ithazhgal (Ambedkarite Journals in Tamil Nadu), published by Neelam Publications, follows journals from the 1930s onward, such as Samathuvam, Udayasuriyan and Madurakavignan [1]. These small papers carried Ambedkar's message of equality to Tamil readers, and his research helps make sure their history is not lost [1].

name: Punitha Pandian
work: Edits Dalit Murasu, a Chennai Tamil monthly that has carried Dalit news and extracts from Ambedkar's writings to Tamil readers.
story: Punitha Pandian edits Dalit Murasu, a Tamil monthly from Chennai that reports on Dalit politics, culture and activism in Tamil Nadu [1][2]. The magazine has carried interviews, book reviews, a series explaining the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and a monthly extract from Dr. Ambedkar's writings [1]. It also published a Tamil translation of Annihilation of Caste, Babasaheb's famous speech against the caste system [1]. At one point supporters had to appeal for donations because the small magazine was close to stopping for lack of money [1]. Described as an Ambedkarite activist of three decades, the editor later served as vice-chairperson of the Tamil Nadu SC/ST Commission, which handled thousands of complaints of caste discrimination [2].

name: Thol. Thirumavalavan
work: Leads the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (Liberation Panthers), a Tamil Dalit movement turned party that draws on Ambedkar, Periyar and Marx.
story: Thirumavalavan worked as a government forensic officer before joining the Dalit Panther Iyakkam, and he took over its leadership after its founder A. Malaichamy died in 1989 [1]. In 1990 the movement became the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK), and until 1999 it stayed away from elections and worked as a social movement [1]. Its ideas draw on Ambedkar's call for social justice, Periyar's rationalism and Marx's focus on working people [1]. The VCK first contested elections in 1999, and Thirumavalavan has since been elected to the Lok Sabha from the Chidambaram reserved seat [1][2]. The party refused to ally with the PMK after the 2012 caste violence in Dharmapuri, backed reservation for backward classes, and in 2020 protested for a ban on the Manusmriti, an old law book that ranks people by caste [1].

name: Gaddar (Gummadi Vittal Rao)
work: Telugu people's balladeer whose songs against caste and inequality moved villages for decades and, in his last years, carried Ambedkarite and constitutional ideas.
story: Born Gummadi Vittal Rao in Toopran in 1949, Gaddar founded the Jana Natya Mandali, a cultural troupe that took songs and street performance from village to village [1][2]. His songs spoke against caste discrimination and economic inequality, and he stood with Dalit families seeking justice after the 1985 Karamchedu massacre [1][2]. He survived an attempt on his life at his home in 1997, though a bullet stayed lodged in his spine, and his songs later gave energy to the movement for a separate Telangana state [1]. His father had been deeply moved by Dr. Ambedkar's speeches, and after Telangana was formed Gaddar openly took up Ambedkarite ideas and spoke up for constitutional values [2]. He died in Hyderabad on 6 August 2023 [1][3].

name: Gogu Shyamala
work: Telugu writer whose stories show the daily lives, work and courage of Dalit Madiga women in Telangana villages.
story: Gogu Shyamala grew up in the Madiga quarter of Peddemul village, the daughter of farm labourers, and she was the only one of her surviving siblings to reach higher education [1]. She studied in a government social welfare hostel and later earned a sociology degree from Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Open University [1]. After the 1991 Tsundur massacre of Dalits, she began reading Ambedkar closely and started questioning how the Left dealt with caste [1]. Her story collection Father May Be an Elephant and Mother Only a Small Basket, But... tells village life from the side of Dalit women, and it reached new readers when Tilted Axis Press republished it [2][3]. She has worked as a senior fellow at the Anveshi Research Centre for Women's Studies in Hyderabad [1].

name: Anil Sarkar
work: Bengali poet and CPI(M) leader who started Tripura's Dalit movement around the 1991 Ambedkar centenary and created Ambedkar awards for students.
story: Anil Sarkar was a Bengali-language poet and a Communist (CPI(M)) leader in Tripura who was elected to the state assembly a record nine times and served as a minister in six Left Front governments [1][2]. In 1991, the year of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's birth centenary, he began serious work to build a Dalit movement in Tripura, and he is seen as the father of Dalit literature in the state [1]. As minister for Scheduled Caste, OBC and minority welfare, he started the Ambedkar Award and the Ambedkar Merit Award, which gave cash and books, including Ambedkarite and Dalit writing, to students who did well in school exams [1]. Forward Press writes that he combined Ambedkar's ideas with Marx's and spread this approach across the North-East over the next 25 years [1]. He was chosen for the Ambedkar National Award in 2000, to be presented at a Dalit Sahitya Akademi conference in Delhi, and he died in February 2015 at the age of 76, having written 24 books [2][3].

name: Kanwal Bharti
work: Hindi Dalit writer from Rampur who brings forgotten Dalit thinkers back into view and writes on Ambedkarite ideas.
story: Kanwal Bharti, born in February 1953, is described by Forward Press as a progressive Ambedkarite thinker and an active writer of the Hindi Dalit movement [1]. His major works include Dalit Sahitya Kee Avdharna, on the idea of Dalit literature, and a collection of the writings of Swami Achootanand Harihar [1]. He writes about earlier Dalit thinkers who are often left out of history, such as Chandrika Prasad Jigyasu and his writing against mental slavery [1]. He received the Dr. Ambedkar Rashtriya Award in 1996 and the Bhimratna Puraskar in 2001 [1]. In 2013 he was arrested in Rampur over a Facebook comment criticising the state government and was released on bail, a case that drew wide criticism [2][3].

name: Omprakash Valmiki
work: Hindi writer whose autobiography Joothan exposed everyday caste cruelty and became a landmark of Dalit literature.
story: Omprakash Valmiki was born in 1950 into a Dalit family in Muzaffarnagar district of Uttar Pradesh, and as a schoolboy he was made to sweep the school grounds by a headmaster because of his caste [1]. He found work in a government ordnance factory and was posted in many parts of India, including Chandrapur district in Maharashtra, where the Ambedkarite movement shaped his outlook [1]. His autobiography Joothan exposed caste oppression so sharply that it drew attacks, and it was later published in English as Joothan: A Dalit's Life [1][2]. He also wrote poetry and books on Dalit literature, and he died on 17 November 2013 [1].

name: Kalyani Thakur Charal
work: Bengali Dalit feminist poet who has edited the little magazine Nir for over 25 years, making room for Dalit women writers.
story: Kalyani Thakur Charal was born in 1965 into the Matua community of Nadia district and worked for Indian Railways for more than two decades while writing [1]. For years she published most of her own work because Bengali publishers showed little interest, and she later wrote a memoir about life as a Dalit woman in the railways [1]. She has edited the little magazine Nir for more than 25 years, and it has become a platform for Dalit women's voices [2]. Her poems speak to Babasaheb Ambedkar and the Matua leader Harichand Thakur, and she reads Bengal's Dalit literature through Ambedkar's belief that a society cannot progress unless its women progress too [1][2]. She is a member of the West Bengal Dalit Sahitya Akademi, and her poems have appeared in English as I Belong to Nowhere [1][2].

name: Manoranjan Byapari
work: Bengali Dalit writer who taught himself to read in jail, pulled a rickshaw, and wrote prize-winning books about refugees and the poor.
story: Manoranjan Byapari, from the Namasudra community, came to India as a child refugee from what was then East Pakistan [1]. Jailed in 1975 at the age of 20, he taught himself to read and write in prison, and afterwards he pulled a rickshaw for about ten years and then worked as a cook in a government school [1][2]. He met the writer Mahasweta Devi while she was a passenger in his rickshaw, and she invited him to write for her journal Bartika [2]. His memoir Itibritte Chandal Jiban won The Hindu award for non-fiction in 2018, and he has written about a dozen novels [2]. In 2020 the West Bengal government made him chair of the state Dalit Sahitya Akademi, and in 2021 he won the Balagarh reserved seat in the state assembly, saying Dalits and the poor must enter politics to change their own lives [1].

name: Basudev Sunani
work: Odia Dalit poet and novelist whose books record caste violence and the lives of the poor in western Odisha.
story: Basudev Sunani was born in 1962 in the hills of western Odisha and began writing poetry early [1][2]. His collection Asprushya (Untouchable, 2001) marked him out as a Dalit poet, and his essay book Dalit, Punjeebaad O Bhumandalikarana looks at Dalits, capitalism and globalisation [1][2]. His poems give attention to goatherds, small farmers and others living in poverty [1]. His novel Padapodi (2014) is based on the January 2012 burning of forty Dalit homes in Lathore village in Bolangir district, and it was published in English in 2025 as Burnt: Beyond Return [3][4]. Reviewers call him a leading voice of modern Odia Dalit literature whose writing and activism record Dalit struggles in Odisha [3].

name: The Community Library Project
place: Khirki Extension and other neighbourhoods, New Delhi, Delhi, India
work: Free neighbourhood libraries in Delhi and Gurugram, inspired by Ambedkar, open to everyone whatever their caste, class or ability.
story: The Community Library Project runs free, open-to-all libraries in Delhi neighbourhoods such as Khirki Extension, Kotla Mubarakpur and South Extension, and in Sikanderpur in Gurugram [1]. The group says it is inspired by Ambedkar and works to include people of every caste, class and ability, with a Reading for Justice shelf of books on gender, caste and disability, including Dalit writing and Braille books [1]. Most members are children and teenagers, many of them the first in their families to go to school, and some teenagers serve as student leaders [1]. The Kotla Mubarakpur library, in the basement of a hall once used for weddings, holds about 11,000 books, and around 60 people signed up on the day the South Extension branch opened in 2023 [1].

sources.title: ThePrint — Delhi has two community libraries that won't discriminate or silence you

name: Jaga Solanki
work: Kutch villager who led a years-long fight to win back land for his community's cremation ground.
story: Jaga Solanki of Ambilayara village near Bachau in Kutch led a struggle of about four years, including sit-ins at government offices, to recover 2.5 acres of land meant for the Dalit cremation ground, part of which a powerful landowner had taken [1]. Even after a court decision in their favour, it was carried out only when police removed the encroaching structure, after the suspicious death of his brother, whom Jaga then buried on that land [1]. Because Dalits were kept out of the village temple, the community built one of its own [1]. Although he cannot read, Jaga knows Ambedkar's ideas well, and he was among more than 110 families in Kutch who embraced Buddhism on 14 October 2019 [1].

sources.title: SabrangIndia — Stories of change-makers in Kutch, Gujarat

name: Nandaben Chauhan
work: Wood seller in Ahmedabad who saved for 15 years to install a bust of Ambedkar in her neighbourhood.
story: Nandaben Chauhan, a 68-year-old Dalit woman in Kochrab village in Ahmedabad, earns her living by selling wood that she buys from the municipality [1]. She put aside money for 15 years to pay for a bust of Ambedkar, shown in a blue coat, red tie and thick-rimmed glasses, on a platform in her area [1]. The bust stands next to a Hanuman temple, a short walk from the Kochrab Ashram that Gandhi founded in 1915 [1].

sources.title: Deccan Herald — Dalit woman saves up for 15 years, installs Ambedkar's statue next to Hanuman temple

name: Savji Vankar
work: Weaver in a Dalit weavers' colony in Kutch whose whole family follows Ambedkar's path and Buddhism.
story: Savji Vankar lives in Vanat Nagar, a weavers' colony of about 60 Dalit families in Kutch, where he runs a family weaving business with his wife, sons and daughter-in-law [1]. The family weaves on contract for a Bhuj-based organisation, and work is uncertain, with some stretches bringing fewer than ten days of paid work [1]. His son Arvind wants direct links with buyers and a strong English education for his own son, so the next generation has more bargaining power [1]. Savji credits Ambedkar for the dignity his family now has, and the whole family follows Buddhism and wants to walk his path [1].

sources.title: SabrangIndia — Stories of change-makers in Kutch, Gujarat

name: H.K. Satish
work: Court clerk who has spent 20 years collecting Ambedkar coins and stamps and shows them in exhibitions around the country.
story: H.K. Satish comes from Mulbagal taluk in Kolar district, studied history, and works as a clerk at the district court in Hassan [1]. For about 20 years he has often set aside half his salary to travel across India collecting rare coins and stamps, especially those linked to Ambedkar [1]. His collection includes about 10,000 Ambedkar-related coins, gathered partly by visiting every state to find the birth-centenary commemorative coin, and every postage stamp issued on Ambedkar [1]. His January 2026 exhibition in Mysuru was his 147th, and he has received a fee or travel costs for only about 20 of them [1].

sources.title: ETV Bharat — Rare Stamps And Coins Exhibition Honouring Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Opens In Mysuru

name: Lakshmamma
work: Dalit woman from Tumakuru who kept an atrocity case alive for 15 years until the Supreme Court upheld the conviction.
story: In August 2008, a group of men from dominant castes attacked the Dalit colony of Dunda village in Tumakuru district with clubs and stones, injuring seven people [1]. When the trial court acquitted everyone in 2011 and the state did not appeal, Lakshmamma and her son Govindaraju took the case to the Karnataka High Court themselves, with help from Bengaluru lawyers and local activists [1]. Her son died in 2016, but she kept going, and in October 2023 the High Court convicted ten of the accused under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, a law that protects Dalits and Adivasis from caste violence; the Supreme Court upheld the verdict in August 2024 [1]. Dalit families in Dunda now work in nearby villages instead of for the landowning castes [1].

sources.title: The News Minute — How a Dalit woman and lawyers waged a 15-year battle to get a conviction in a caste crime

name: Buddha Vihara community libraries of North Nagpur
work: Neighbourhood libraries set up in or above Buddhist viharas in North Nagpur's bastis, turning places of worship into places of study.
story: In the bastis (low-income settlements) of North Nagpur, several Buddha viharas, the meeting halls of Ambedkarite Buddhists, now also hold small libraries, some in a separate room and some on the floor above the shrine [1]. In writer Sumit Jambhulkar's own basti, the vihara committee pushed for a community hall, a process that can take more than two years, and turned it into a library [1]. Only a few students came at first, but numbers grew steadily, which matters in an area where many children drop out after Class 8 or 9 [1]. Residents see this as following Ambedkar, who founded the Buddhist Society of India in 1955 and wanted viharas to become centres of knowledge and development, not only of worship [1].

sources.title: Round Table India — The Buddha Vihara as a centre of knowledge: Community libraries in slums

name: Dr. Ulhas Wagh
work: Doctor who runs a free health tent every 6 December for the huge crowds who come to Mumbai to honour Babasaheb.
story: Every 6 December, tens of thousands of people, many of them poor farm workers, travel to Shivaji Park and Chaitya Bhoomi in Mumbai to mark the anniversary of Ambedkar's death [1]. Dr. Ulhas Wagh heads a free health tent there, bringing a team of 12 to 15 doctors each year [1]. In one day the team sees about 4,000 people with problems such as headaches, skin rashes and stomach upsets [1]. Many arrive weak from long journeys and hunger, so his tent quietly looks after the people who come to remember Babasaheb [1].

sources.title: PARI — What no one could do, Ambedkar did

name: Kusumtai Sonawane
work: Village activist in the Pune hills who keeps Ambedkar's story alive through women's songs and by teaching children.
story: Kusumtai Sonawane, a woman in her 70s from Nandgaon village in Mulshi taluka of Pune district, is an activist with the Garib Dongri Sanghatana, a group that works with poor families in the district's hilly areas [1]. Every April the women of Nandgaon sing songs for Ambedkar Jayanti, including a lullaby by a farmer-poet who studied only until Class 4, and the celebrations move from village to village until Buddha Purnima [1]. Kusumtai teaches local children about Babasaheb's life so that they remember how hard he worked to unite people in the fight for equal rights [1]. When PARI reached her during the 2020 lockdown, she was harvesting gram in the fields and worried that promised free rations had not arrived [1].

sources.title: PARI — Ambedkar: The diamond that lit up the sky

name: M.M. Shaikh
work: Bookseller from Beed who sets up a stall of books on caste and society at the 6 December gathering in Mumbai.
story: M.M. Shaikh sells books in Beed town in Marathwada, and he also travels to Mumbai's Shivaji Park for the 6 December gathering held in Ambedkar's memory [1]. There he lays out two long tables of books, mostly on social and caste questions, for visitors who come from villages across Maharashtra [1]. He told PARI that he comes every year, though on the rainy day of the 2017 report he had sold almost nothing and planned to pack up early and head home that night [1].

sources.title: PARI — What no one could do, Ambedkar did

name: Meera Umap
work: Folk singer who plays the dimadi drum and sings Bhim geet, songs that carry Babasaheb's message, across Marathwada.
story: Meera Umap was born around 1965 into a poor Matang family, a Dalit community, in Antarwali village of Beed district, and she never went to school [1]. As a child she travelled with her parents as they sang devotional songs for alms, taught herself the dimadi, a small drum, by tapping on water pots, and later became a shahir, a singer of folk ballads [1]. Since about 1991, the centenary of Ambedkar's birth, she has focused on Bhim geet, songs that thank Babasaheb and share his ideas, and she also performs skits against addiction and dowry [1]. Despite many awards she has had little money or support, and when her house burned down in 2020, fellow Ambedkarites helped her build a new tin-walled home [1].

sources.title: PARI (People's Archive of Rural India) — Meera Umap: singing in the change

name: Radhabai Borhade
work: Former farm worker from Beed whose grindmill songs about Ambedkar, the Buddha and equality are preserved by PARI.
story: Radhabai Borhade lived in Bhim Nagar, the Dalit hamlet of Majalgaon in Beed district, where she worked as a farm labourer and later ran a small grocery shop [2]. She sings ovi, short folk verses that women traditionally sang while grinding grain, and her songs were recorded in 1996 for PARI's Grindmill Songs Project and revisited in 2017 [1][2]. Her verses celebrate Ambedkar's birth in Mhow and his fight against caste, retell the Buddha's story, and describe her community's Buddhist identity as one of dignity [1][2]. She is deeply interested in Ambedkar and Buddhist teachings and has visited Ajanta and Ellora, Mhow, and Deekshabhoomi in Nagpur, where Ambedkar embraced Buddhism in 1956 [2].

name: Sunil Yadav
work: Third-generation Mumbai municipal sanitation worker who studied up to an MPhil while working, to speak up for fellow sweepers.
story: Sunil Yadav was born in 1979 in a Mumbai slum and joined the city's municipal corporation in 2005, the third generation of his family to work as a sweeper, with tasks that included cleaning drains [2]. After failing Class 10, he returned to studying while still working and earned degrees in commerce, journalism and social work, and in 2016 an MPhil from the Tata Institute of Social Sciences [1][2]. His mother, influenced by Ambedkar through her own father, pushed for her children's education, and Sunil says he discovered Ambedkar for himself in 2005 [2]. He chose to stay in his job and has said he wants to study why sweepers are kept on the margins and help them understand and fight for their rights [1].

name: Vennila Suresh Kumar
work: Domestic worker in Dharavi who co-founded a women's self-help group and helps lead the neighbourhood's yearly march for Ambedkar.
story: Vennila Suresh Kumar's family came to Mumbai's Dharavi from Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu, and she studied until Class 9 and learned English while working as a domestic worker [1]. In 2016 she co-founded a women's self-help group, Magizhchi Magalir Peravai, which supports local women and gave out food, groceries and small sums of money during the Covid lockdown [1]. She and her husband Suresh, a driver, are part of the Jai Bhim Foundation, which since 2012 has led a candlelit march with parai drums and blue flags to Dharavi's Ambedkar statue on 6 December, the anniversary of his death, known as Mahaparinirvan Diwas [1]. At the march she gathers women and sings Tamil songs about Babasaheb's work, and her family embraced Buddhism the year before the 2023 report [1].

sources.title: PARI — Dharavi's Bhim celebrations

name: Vijay Surwade
work: Retired bank manager who has spent about 50 years building a private archive of photographs, letters and objects linked to Babasaheb.
story: Vijay Surwade first heard about Ambedkar from his grandfather in Usawad village in Jalgaon district, and as a schoolboy he pasted magazine cuttings of Ambedkar's photos and speeches into a notebook [2]. Working in the evenings beside his job as a bank manager and using his own savings, he travelled to almost every state in search of old photographs, negatives, letters and documents [1][2]. His collection, kept in boxes and files in his flat, includes a rare photograph of Ramabai Ambedkar traced to a Nagpur studio and personal items such as Ambedkar's spectacles [1][2]. He has written more than 17 books from this material and hopes to turn his home into a research library or trust, because he feels Dalits must preserve their own history [1][2].

sources.title: Scroll (Thomson Reuters Foundation) — This is our history. No one else will preserve it: How Dalits are archiving caste history
Homegrown — Intimate Pieces Of BR Ambedkar's Life Are Alive & Well In Kalyan

name: Vikas Tatad
work: Young educator from Amravati's Bhim Nagar who started a low-fee pre-primary school named in the spirit of Ambedkar's education work.
story: While studying at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences in 2016, Vikas Tatad realised that very few people in his home neighbourhood of Bhim Nagar in Amravati had college degrees [1]. He first ran an informal school called Mission Education for about 150 students, and later, while doing a Master's at Columbia University's Teachers College, used prize money to start the People's International School for nursery and kindergarten children [1]. The school asks only a voluntary fee of Rs 500, trains its teachers in modern methods, and uses a roundtable style where teachers and children sit as equals [1]. Its name echoes Ambedkar's People's Education Society, and its foundation was laid on 19 June, the date in 1950 when Ambedkar laid the foundation of Milind College in Aurangabad [1].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — Columbia University Student Launches People's International School to Address Educational Disparities in Maharashtra

name: Kalinga Mitra Trust and Bijay Kumar Nag
work: Odisha students who return from universities to their villages to support young people and share anti-caste history.
story: In 2012, a village youth named Bijay Kumar Nag returned home to Odisha after training at the Nagarjuna Training Institute in Nagpur and introduced younger people, including the writer Manoj Bag, to Ambedkar's call to educate, agitate and organise [1]. Bijay became the first student from that village to study outside Odisha, later joining the University of Hyderabad [1]. Students like him who came back from Nagpur and went on to central universities founded the Kalinga Mitra Trust, which supports marginalised students and anti-caste work [1]. These young scholars spend their holidays holding talks, film screenings and Ambedkar Jayanti events in villages and helping students prepare for entrance exams [1].

sources.title: Round Table India — Dalit Scholars Take Anti-caste Movement and Politics from Academia to Villages

name: Madhusudan
place: Ambedkar Nagar (Lanjipalli area), Brahmapur, Odisha, India
work: Dalit activist who led a motorcycle journey through Odisha villages to record caste atrocities and tell people about their rights.
story: Inspired by Kanshi Ram's earlier cycle journeys, Madhusudan, a Dalit social activist from Ambedkar Nagar village near Brahmapur in Odisha, started a motorcycle yatra (journey) on 6 December 2022, the anniversary of Ambedkar's death [1]. It began with 35 riders and was planned to end on 14 April 2023, Ambedkar's birthday [1]. The riders visited homes to hear complaints, recorded stories of caste atrocities to build a record of them, and worked with officials to seek justice for Dalit and Adivasi families [1]. In its first weeks the yatra covered about 1,100 km and met people across a dozen villages, aiming to make everyone aware of their rights [1].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — Motorcycle diaries tell untold stories of Dalit atrocities

name: Dalit women of Ballad Kalan (Manpreet Kaur, Harmer Kaur and others)
work: Landless Dalit women in Sangrur who won their community's share of village common land and now farm it together.
story: In Punjab, part of each village's common land is meant to be leased to Dalit families, but it was often grabbed through proxy bidders, and the Zameen Prapti Sangharsh Committee (land rights struggle committee) has organised Dalits in Sangrur district to claim it [1][2]. In Ballad Kalan, women led the fight: Harmer Kaur was beaten by police during a 2014 protest over the land auction, and Manpreet Kaur's house became the movement's planning room [1]. After the women uprooted paddy planted on a plot held by a proxy, the lease was auctioned again and Dalits won it as a group for the first time, pooling their money to pay [1]. Families now earn about Rs 30,000 a year from the land, plus grain and fodder, and the report places this struggle in Punjab's long history of Dalit awakening shaped by Ambedkar and Kanshi Ram [1].

sources.title: SabrangIndia (IndiaSpend) — Fist For Farm: How Punjab's Dalits Are Fighting For Their Right Over Common Land
The Caravan — A Growing Movement in Jhaloor Illustrates How Dalit Villagers in Punjab Are Reclaiming Their Right to Panchayat Land

name: Samvidhanik Vichar Manch (Gigraj Jodli)
work: Village youth group in Sikar that put the Preamble on a school plaque so that children read it every day.
story: Samvidhanik Vichar Manch, meaning Constitutional Thought Forum, is a youth collective started by Gigraj Jodli in Jodli village of Sikar district, Rajasthan [1]. By 2022 it had been active for about two years and had installed a plaque with the Preamble, the opening statement of the Constitution's ideals, at the government school on the village's main road [1]. Students receive copies of the Preamble and read it every day [1]. The group's aim is that every household and every child in the village knows the rights the Constitution promises them [1].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — Rajasthan: The preamble of the constitution is taught to the children in the village school every day

name: Amrutham (Amrutham Amma)
work: Dalit woman panchayat president who insisted on her right to hoist the national flag in her own village.
story: Amrutham, a 62-year-old Dalit woman, was elected in 2019 as an independent to lead Athupakkam panchayat (village council) in Tiruvallur district, in a seat reserved for Scheduled Castes [1]. Some local leaders from dominant castes did not want her to hoist the national flag, and she was stopped on Republic Day and again on Independence Day in 2020 [1]. She kept complaining to officials, the panchayat secretary was suspended, and on 20 August 2020 she hoisted the flag at the panchayat office with the district Collector and police chief beside her [1]. She said she wanted to get on with fixing roads, lights and water supply and helping homeless and jobless people, and asked why a Scheduled Caste leader should be stopped from serving [1].

sources.title: The News Minute — How a Dalit woman leader asserted her right, hoisted tricolour on August 20

name: Samathuva Padipagam (Aindhupanai village collective)
work: Students and graduates who run an Ambedkar-Periyar library and free evening tuition in their Tamil Nadu village.
story: In 2018, P Rajkumar, a young IT analyst from Aindhupanai, asked the local government for space for a library, and a collective of students and graduates called Samathuva Padipagam opened it in 2019 [1]. The panchayat (village council) lent a community hall, villagers paid for cupboards and furniture and gave books, and the collection grew from about 50 books to a few hundred [1]. Volunteers keep it open through the day, and before the pandemic they ran evening tuition for more than 30 government school students, along with a coding course and informal career advice [1]. The library is named after Ambedkar and Periyar, keeps their original writings, and aims to build social justice and political awareness among young people [1].

sources.title: The News Minute — Growing book by book: How a TN village came together to run an Ambedkar-Periyar Library

name: Thudi movement (Bharathi Prabhu)
work: Tamil Nadu group that holds yearly graduation ceremonies celebrating Dalit graduates and planned Ambedkar night schools and libraries.
story: Activist Bharathi Prabhu first tried in 2009 to hold a graduation ceremony for Dalit students, modelled on the ceremonies Black Americans hold to celebrate their graduates [1]. By its tenth edition in February 2019, the Thudi movement's ceremony drew about a hundred Dalit graduates from across Tamil Nadu, including Chennai's resettlement colonies, and also honoured achievers in arts, sports, medicine and activism [1]. Prabhu says most stories about Dalits focus only on suffering, and the event is meant to bring success and representation into public view [1]. He sees it as carrying on Ambedkar's legacy, and to mark the tenth year the group planned 100 Dr. Ambedkar Night Schools and 100 Savitribai Phule Libraries across the state [1].

sources.title: The News Minute — How this graduation ceremony in TN is changing narratives around Dalit representation

name: Vyasai Thozhargal
work: North Chennai youth group running a free tuition centre named after Ambedkar and standing with local workers and residents.
story: Vyasai Thozhargal, meaning Comrades of Vyasarpadi, is a group of first-generation graduates who, around 2016, started a free after-school tuition centre on a rooftop for children in their area [1]. Called Dr Ambedkar Pagutharivu Padasalai, it now has about 40 volunteers, a teacher for each class, a small computer lab, healthy snacks and sports such as kabaddi, silambam and chess, and it serves hundreds of children [1]. A student from its first batch went on to college and now teaches there, and the centre says its students have passed all their subjects for years [1]. The group also teaches Ambedkar's writings, runs student parliament elections to teach democracy, and has stood with sanitation workers and recorded pollution disasters in north Chennai, in the spirit of his call to educate, agitate and organise [2].

sources.title: Citizen Matters — How a tuition centre in Chennai's Vyasarpadi is helping keep children in schools
The News Minute — How north Chennai youth are answering Ambedkar's call to educate, agitate, and organise

name: Amit Gautam
work: Runs a free library and coaching centre for Dalit and poor children, and for women, in his village near Prayagraj.
story: After his studies at Allahabad University, Amit Gautam saw that many children in his village struggled with basic reading, so he began teaching them, at first in open spaces [1]. On 3 January 2022, Savitribai Phule's birth anniversary, he opened a proper library and coaching space with about 2,000 books, paid for through online crowdfunding, donated books and free labour from villagers [1]. About 400 people use it, roughly 300 children and 100 women, and volunteers teach maths, English and computers, along with lessons on Bahujan heroes (leaders from communities long pushed to the margins) and menstrual hygiene for girls [1]. He says he follows Savitribai Phule's example and Babasaheb Ambedkar's ideals, and he has carried on even after facing rumours and a false police case [1].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — I am undeterred by these intimidations as my inspiration is Savitri Bai Phule: Amit Gautam

name: Ashok Kumar Baudh
work: Lucknow wall painter who rides a decorated motorbike carrying a model of the Constitution to start conversations about citizens' rights.
story: Ashok Kumar Baudh, a wall painter in Lucknow, says he grew up knowing nothing about the Constitution until he heard a poetic version of it set to music [1]. He then fitted his motorcycle with a frame he calls his Rath (chariot), which carries a model of the Constitution and portraits of Babasaheb Ambedkar and Kanshi Ram [1]. He stops to talk with curious people about the fundamental rights in Part III of the Constitution, paints wall advertisements for the musical version without being paid, and in 2023 was organising a bike rally for Constitution Day on 26 November [1]. He wants everyone who has gained from the Constitution to help spread it, and he has kept going despite opposition, including someone puncturing his tyre [1].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — Constitution Month Special: Meet the Man Wearing Ashok Chakra and Spreading Gospel of Constitution

name: Govind Singh
work: Village teacher with a disability who tutors young children and teaches them about Phule, Ambedkar and the Constitution.
story: Govind Singh of Makrandpur village in Jalaun was born with a disability, and when a medical treatment failed in 2008 he gave up his MA studies and returned home [1]. He decided to give his life to teaching children of his community from kindergarten to Class 5, helping with school revision and with the lives and ideas of Jyotiba Phule and Ambedkar [1]. About 500 students have learned with him, and many of them now tutor younger children themselves [1]. He belongs to the Bundelkhand Dalit Adhikar Manch, a rights group whose Jai Bhim Education Centre offers daily classwork and constitutional studies [1], and which campaigns across Bundelkhand to spread constitutional values and care for neglected Ambedkar statues in villages [2].

sources.title: The Mooknayak — Empowering Through Education: Differently-Abled Teacher's Commitment to Ambedkarite Ideology

name: Ram Laut Baudh
work: Retired railway worker on a mission to place printed copies of the Constitution in one lakh (100,000) homes.
story: Ram Laut Baudh, a retired railway employee in Lucknow, has set himself the goal of giving printed copies of the Indian Constitution to one lakh homes [1]. He believes a real book in the house starts more family conversations than a PDF file, which can easily be lost [1]. He traces his inspiration to a visit to the garden in Baroda where, on 23 September 1917, Ambedkar resolved to work for the uplift of oppressed communities [1]. He calls the Preamble, the opening statement of the Constitution's ideals, its soul, and he sees his work as carrying Babasaheb's mission forward [1].

name: Ravi Yadav
work: Former policeman who runs free classes on school subjects, Bahujan history and the Constitution in 32 villages near Lucknow.
story: Ravi Yadav, a former police officer from Janpur near Lucknow, started the Dr. Bhim Rao Ambedkar Shikshan Sansthan, an education institute, around late 2022 [1]. Its classes run in 32 villages, helping children with their school syllabus on weekdays and teaching Bahujan heroes, history, culture and the Constitution at weekends, along with physical training [1]. Younger children learn basic constitutional ideas while older students study procedural laws, and there are no fees, only small voluntary gifts from parents [1]. Yadav calls himself an Ambedkarite and says the Constitution is what secured rights for his own community too [1].
